The module receives audio from a phone or PC over Bluetooth (A2DP), and two modules can play together as a True Wireless Stereo pair. The Bluetooth input is selected like any other input; the status LED is blue whenever it is active.

    What True Wireless Stereo does on the JP150, and the words used for it.

  • TWS: pairing two units

    The procedure for two new units, step by step, and how to check the result.

  • TWS: everyday use

    Switching on, power-up order, common tasks such as swapping the roles.

  • TWS: status and troubleshooting

    The status values, what to do when the units do not pair, known limitations.

  • LED reference

    Every Bluetooth and TWS pattern of the status LED.

The TWS pages are the content of the TWS User Guide 1.0 (2026-09-21), written for firmware 26.9.0 and later. Firmware 26.8.0 and earlier handles TWS differently and does not behave as described.

docs.title: Connect a phone
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

  1. Select the Bluetooth input on the module (the encoder button, the Bluetooth tile on MuraLink's Overview, or SYS:INPUT): the status LED turns blue and breathes calmly while no phone is connected.
  2. On the phone, open the Bluetooth settings and connect to the module. The module appears under its Bluetooth name; how to read or change it is below.
  3. Start playback. The status LED is solid blue while the phone is connected without audio and shows a slow heartbeat while audio streams.

The module supports the SBC, AAC and LDAC codecs. A paired phone reconnects by itself when both are in range. For two modules playing together, see TWS: about and terms.

docs.title: Bluetooth and TWS LED reference
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 True Wireless Stereo (TWS) User Guide, revision 1.1 · 615 kB

When the Bluetooth input is selected, the status LED shows the Bluetooth and TWS state. Blue is always present: it identifies the Bluetooth input. Pulse speed and the second colour tell what the unit is doing:

  • Fast pulse (about 500 ms): in progress (pairing, connecting, searching).
  • Slow pulse (about 2.5 s): settled or linked.
  • Steady: connected and idle.
  • Two-colour alternation: TWS is engaged; the accent colour encodes the role (green = Primary, purple-red = Secondary).
LED pattern Meaning Solid blue Phone connected, no audio. Slow blue heartbeat (mostly bright) Phone streaming audio. Fast blue pulse Phone pairing or connecting. Calm blue breathe Bluetooth input selected, idle (no phone, no TWS). Hard 1.5 s blue blink Bluetooth module not responding. Fast blue and green TWS Primary is searching for a Secondary. Slow blue and green TWS Primary linked to the Secondary. Fast blue and purple-red TWS Secondary is waiting for a Primary. Slow blue and purple-red TWS Secondary linked to the Primary.

The role colour follows the unit's Fallback Role. When the input is not Bluetooth, the status LED shows the input colour instead (Indicators and LEDs). The brief moment after the Bluetooth input is selected, before the Bluetooth module reports its state, shows the calm blue breathe.

docs.title: TWS: about and terms
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.9.02026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 True Wireless Stereo (TWS) User Guide, revision 1.1 · 615 kB

Two JP150 units can play the same audio from a single Bluetooth host, with no cable between them. This feature is called True Wireless Stereo (TWS). Both units must run the same firmware version, 26.9.0 or newer, and the matching MuraLink.

docs.title: About TWS
docs.text:
Normally a host (for example a smartphone) connects to one amplifier over Bluetooth, and that amplifier plays the audio. With TWS, two amplifiers work as a pair:

  • The host connects to only one of them: the Primary unit.
  • The Primary plays the audio and also relays it wirelessly to the second unit: the Secondary.
  • Both units play in sync, so you can drive two speakers, or speakers in two rooms, from one host.
  • The two units remember each other. After the first pairing you do not need to pair them again: every time they are switched on, they find each other automatically.

In the current firmware both units play the full stereo signal. To make one unit play only the left channel and the other only the right channel, configure the channel routing on each unit separately, for example in its ADAU1452 DSP program.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning TWS (True Wireless Stereo) Two Bluetooth audio devices linked so that they play audio from a single source in sync. Unit One JP150 amplifier module. The procedures refer to the two units of a pair as unit A and unit B. Host (Bluetooth host) The Bluetooth audio source, such as a smartphone or PC. Peer The other unit of the pair. From the point of view of unit A, unit B is its peer, and vice versa. Primary The unit that the host connects to. It receives the audio from the host, plays it, and relays it to the Secondary. Secondary The unit that receives the audio from the Primary instead of from the host. Pairing (bond) The stored link information that allows the two units to recognise and reconnect to each other. Each unit keeps its own copy in the non-volatile memory of its Bluetooth module, so the pairing survives power cycles. Clearing the pairing on one unit does not clear it on the other. Remembered peer The peer whose pairing is stored on a unit. A unit with a stored pairing is said to remember its peer. TWS capability The main TWS on/off switch of a unit. When TWS is disabled, the unit works only as a standalone Bluetooth amplifier. The setting takes effect immediately but is not retained after a restart: at every power-up the unit sets it automatically, based on the remembered peer and the Fallback role. Fallback role The role that a unit takes at power-up if it does not remember a peer: Standalone (TWS is not used), Primary (factory default: the unit actively searches for a unit to pair with) or Secondary (the unit waits to be found by a searching unit). The Fallback role applies only when no peer is remembered. If a peer is remembered, the unit reconnects to it and ignores the Fallback role. Current role The role that the unit currently has in the active TWS link: Primary, Secondary, or Unknown if no peer information is available yet. Boot outcome Records what happened to TWS at the unit's most recent power-up (status values). TWS status The live state of the link to the peer (status values). Peer memory The list of paired devices stored in a unit's Bluetooth module. It contains both the hosts that you have paired and the TWS peer, which is marked in the list. MuraLink shows this list in the Peer table.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• MuraLink on a Windows PC, the version that matches the unit firmware. MuraLink communicates with one unit at a time, so you configure the units one after the other.
  • Firmware 26.9.0 or newer on both units (Firmware updates).
  • Two JP150 modules, each with a power supply and speakers connected, and two USB-C data cables (charge-only cables do not work).
  • Recommended: an external Bluetooth antenna on each module, for better range.
  • A smartphone or other Bluetooth audio source (the host).

No additional hardware setup is required for TWS. Place the two units within Bluetooth range of each other, and the Primary within range of the host.

Tip

Put a small label on each unit (for example "A – Primary" and "B – Secondary") so that you always know which unit the host connects to.

docs.title: TWS: controls in MuraLink
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.9.02026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 True Wireless Stereo (TWS) User Guide, revision 1.1 · 615 kB

Connect a unit to the PC through its USB DATA connector and start MuraLink. Select the unit's COM port and click Connect. Then open Bluetooth > TWS in the sidebar: the TWS (True Wireless Stereo) settings and status at the top, the remembered devices below.

docs.title: TWS settings and status
docs.text: Bluetooth > TWS: the settings and the status at the top, the remembered devices below. Element Description TWS capability: Enable / Disable A two-button switch. The selected (dark) button shows the current state; only the other button can be clicked. When TWS is disabled, all other controls in the TWS section are greyed out. Immediately after MuraLink connects it can take a moment before either button appears selected. Fallback role: Standalone / Primary / Secondary Three joined buttons; the selected button shows the stored Fallback role. Clicking a different button opens the Change TWS fallback role dialog with three options. OK saves the new role in the unit; it takes effect the next time the unit restarts, and until then a red message reads "A fallback-role change is pending. Reboot or power-cycle the device to apply it." Apply now saves the role and immediately restarts the unit's Bluetooth module: Bluetooth audio stops for a few seconds, and any existing TWS link is dropped. Cancel discards the change. Clicking the role that is already selected has no effect. The Fallback role applies only when no peer is remembered. TWS status, Current role, Paired peer, Boot outcome Status fields, explained on status and troubleshooting. Paired peer shows the Bluetooth address of the remembered peer, or n/a if no peer is remembered. Restart notice While the Bluetooth module restarts (after Apply now or Start new pairing) the section shows "The Bluetooth module is restarting. Values shown are not current." Wait until the notice disappears; this normally takes about 5 seconds. "Remembered peer did not respond" banner Appears when the unit remembers a peer, but the peer did not respond at power-up. The banner has its own Start new pairing button and disappears as soon as the peer connects. TWS Command Console (expert mode) Opens a separate window for developers and system integrators. Not needed for normal use; see the command console.

docs.title: Remembered devices
docs.text: Element Description Summary line and Refresh The summary shows how many devices the unit remembers and how many of these are TWS peers, for example "2 device(s) remembered, 1 of them a TWS peer." MuraLink reads the list when it connects and then every few seconds while the Bluetooth > TWS page is open. Refresh reads it immediately; until the list arrives the table shows "Loading…". Table One row per remembered device, with the columns # (slot number), MAC (Bluetooth address), TWS (marks the TWS peer) and Name. Hosts such as phones usually show their name; the TWS peer usually has no name and is marked in the TWS column. Disconnect Disconnects the TWS link to the peer but keeps the pairing, so that the two units can reconnect later. Reconnect Reconnects the unit to its remembered peer, for example after Disconnect. The link is restored within a few seconds and TWS status changes accordingly. If reconnection is not possible, the status bar at the bottom of the MuraLink window shows the reason: the peer is already connected, no peer is remembered, or TWS is disabled. Forget peer Disconnects the peer and erases the pairing on this unit only. You are asked to confirm. The status bar then shows "TWS peer forgotten." and the TWS row disappears from the table. Start new pairing Clears the TWS pairing and starts pairing again. After you confirm: the currently selected Fallback role is saved, any connected host is disconnected, the remembered peer is forgotten, the Bluetooth module restarts, and the Fallback role is applied (a Primary unit starts searching, a Secondary unit starts waiting). The sequence takes about 5 seconds; only the Bluetooth module restarts, the rest of the unit keeps running. Because Start new pairing always uses the currently selected Fallback role, select the role first and then click Start new pairing.

docs.title: TWS: everyday use
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.9.02026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 True Wireless Stereo (TWS) User Guide, revision 1.1 · 615 kB

docs.title: Switching on
docs.text:
Switch on both units. Each unit finds its remembered peer and reconnects, usually within a few seconds; Boot outcome then shows Reconnected. If a host was connected in the previous session, the connection to the host is normally restored automatically once the TWS link is established.

Power-up order does not matter. If one unit is switched on later, even several minutes later, the two units reconnect automatically within a few seconds. You do not need to restart the unit that was already on.

Secondary switched off during playback. If you switch the Secondary off and on again, it rejoins the Primary and resumes playback automatically.

Only one unit switched on. A unit whose peer remains switched off works on its own. After about 15 seconds its Boot outcome changes to PeerUnreachable, and MuraLink shows the "Remembered peer did not respond" banner. The unit keeps its pairing and does not search for a different peer. As soon as you switch on the other unit, the two units link up.

Host and a lone unit. If a paired unit is switched on alone, the connection to the host is not restored automatically. Connect from the host's Bluetooth settings instead; the connection then works normally. When the other unit is switched on later, it joins, and both units play.

docs.title: Pause and resume the TWS link
docs.text: In the Remembered devices section, click Disconnect. The TWS link is dropped and each unit works on its own, but the pairing is kept. To resume, click Reconnect. The link is restored within a few seconds, and TWS status changes to Connected or Streaming.

docs.title: Swap the Primary and Secondary roles
docs.text:
1. Connect MuraLink to the unit that is to become the Secondary. Set Fallback role to Secondary (click OK in the dialog), and then click Start new pairing and confirm.
  2. Connect MuraLink to the unit that is to become the Primary. Set Fallback role to Primary (click OK), and then click Start new pairing and confirm.
  3. Switch off both units. Switch on the new Secondary first, and the new Primary a few seconds later.
  4. Pair the host with the new Primary.

Changing only the Fallback role is not enough while the units remember each other: they reconnect to each other and ignore the Fallback role. Start new pairing clears the existing pairing so that the new roles take effect.

docs.title: Pair a unit with a different unit
docs.text: Set one unit of the new pair to Primary and the other to Secondary, and run Start new pairing on both units, as described in pairing two units. If the previous partner unit will still be used, also clear its pairing with Forget peer or Start new pairing, so that it does not keep trying to reconnect.

docs.title: Use a unit as a standalone amplifier again
docs.text:
1. In the Remembered devices section, click Forget peer and confirm.
  2. Set Fallback role to Standalone and click OK.
  3. If the other unit is also to be used on its own, repeat steps 1 and 2 on that unit.

At the next power-up the unit finds no remembered peer, follows the Standalone role, and TWS remains off.

Note

Clicking Disable under TWS capability also switches TWS off immediately, but only until the unit restarts. For a permanent change, follow the steps above.

docs.title: Old hosts in the peer list
docs.text: The Peer table also lists paired hosts. MuraLink cannot delete individual host pairings from a unit. To stop an old host from connecting, remove the unit from that host's Bluetooth settings. Forget peer removes only the TWS peer, never hosts.

docs.title: TWS: pairing two units
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.9.02026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 True Wireless Stereo (TWS) User Guide, revision 1.1 · 615 kB

The recommended procedure for two units that have no TWS peer in their peer memory, such as new units. The controls are described on TWS: controls in MuraLink.

Before you start

Switch off Bluetooth on the host, or make sure that the host is not connected to either unit. A unit cannot start TWS pairing while a host is connected to it. You connect the host at the end of the procedure.

docs.title: Step 1: set up unit A as Primary
docs.text:
1. Connect to unit A. Switch it on, connect its USB DATA connector to the PC, start MuraLink, select the unit's COM port, and click Connect.
  2. Check the input. On the Overview tab, make sure that the Bluetooth input is selected. The unit plays Bluetooth audio only when its input is set to Bluetooth.
  3. Open the TWS section. Open Bluetooth > TWS in the sidebar.
  4. Enable TWS. Under TWS capability, check that Enable is selected. If Disable is selected, click Enable.
  5. Set the role. Under Fallback role, click Primary. If the Change TWS fallback role dialog opens, click OK. If Primary is already selected (the factory default), nothing happens; continue with the next step.
  6. Start pairing. In the Remembered devices section, click Start new pairing and confirm with OK. This clears any TWS peer left over from earlier use, and the unit starts searching as Primary. Wait until the message "The Bluetooth module is restarting…" disappears.
  7. Check the peer list. The Peer table must not contain a row marked TWS, and Paired peer must show n/a.
  8. Disconnect MuraLink. Click Disconnect at the top of the MuraLink window (not the Disconnect button in the Remembered devices section) and unplug the USB cable. Leave unit A switched on.

docs.title: Step 2: set up unit B as Secondary
docs.text:
Important

New units are set to Primary by default. One of the two units must be set to Secondary: two Primary units both search for a peer and never find each other.

  1. Connect to unit B. Switch it on, connect its USB DATA connector to the PC, select the unit's COM port in MuraLink, and click Connect.
  2. Check the input. On the Overview tab, select the Bluetooth input.
  3. Enable TWS. On the Bluetooth > TWS page, make sure that Enable is selected under TWS capability.
  4. Set the role. Under Fallback role, click Secondary, and then click OK in the dialog.
  5. Start pairing. In the Remembered devices section, click Start new pairing and confirm with OK. Wait until the restart notice disappears.
  6. Check the peer list. The Peer table must not contain a row marked TWS, unless the units have already paired (see the note below).

Note

If unit A is still switched on, it is already searching for a peer, so the two units usually pair on their own within a few seconds after step 5. A row marked TWS then appears in the Peer table. In that case, skip Step 3 and check the result as described in Step 4.

docs.title: Step 3: let the units find each other
docs.text:
The most reliable way to pair the units is to restart them in the following order:

  1. Switch off both units.
  2. Switch on unit B (Secondary).
  3. A few seconds later, switch on unit A (Primary).

Unit B waits for a peer, unit A searches for and finds unit B, and the pairing is stored on both units. This usually takes a few seconds, but can take up to about 30 seconds.

Switching on both units at the same time also works. Alternatively, with both units switched on, run Start new pairing on unit B first and then on unit A: unit A starts searching immediately, while unit B is already waiting.

docs.title: Step 4: check the result
docs.text:
Connect MuraLink to either unit and open the Bluetooth > TWS page. You should see the following:

Field Unit A Unit B TWS status Connected (or Streaming while audio is playing) Connected (or Streaming) Current role Primary Secondary Paired peer the Bluetooth address of unit B the Bluetooth address of unit A Peer table a row marked TWS a row marked TWS

If this is what you see, pairing is complete and stored on both units. You do not need to pair these units again.

docs.title: Checking the pair without a PC: status LED
docs.text:
When a unit's input is set to Bluetooth, its status LED also indicates TWS activity. The pattern always includes blue. The second colour depends on the unit's Fallback role: green for Primary, purple-red for Secondary.

While a host is connected but the TWS link is not yet established, the LED shows the standard Bluetooth patterns instead: solid blue when connected and idle, and a slow blue heartbeat while audio is playing. A slow, hard blue blink means that the Bluetooth module is not responding. The complete table is on LED reference.

docs.title: Connecting the Bluetooth host
docs.text:
1. Enable Bluetooth on the host.
  2. Pair the host with the Primary unit (unit A). The unit appears under its Bluetooth name, which MuraLink shows as Device Name in the Diagnostics group.
  3. Start playback on the host. Both units play the audio.

Always connect the host to the Primary. The Secondary receives its audio from the Primary, not from the host, and should not appear on the host as a device available for connection.

Tip

To give the units recognisable Bluetooth names, use Change name on Bluetooth > Status. Use only unaccented letters (A to Z), digits and spaces.

docs.title: TWS: status and troubleshooting
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.9.02026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 True Wireless Stereo (TWS) User Guide, revision 1.1 · 615 kB

docs.title: TWS status
docs.text:
• Standby: TWS is enabled, but there is currently no link to the peer. Standby is also shown after TWS has been disabled.
  • Connecting: the unit is trying to connect to its peer.
  • Connected: the link to the peer is established.
  • Streaming: the link is established and audio is being streamed.
  • Unsupported: the Bluetooth module does not report TWS support. This value normally appears only briefly while the Bluetooth module is starting up, or when the module is not responding (see troubleshooting below).

docs.title: Current role
docs.text:
• Primary / Secondary: the unit's role in the active TWS link.
  • Unknown: no peer information is available yet. This is normal after a restart or after the peer has been forgotten, and does not indicate a fault.

docs.title: Boot outcome
docs.text:
• Pending: the unit is still determining its TWS state after power-up. The value usually settles within about 15 seconds.
  • NoPeer: no peer was remembered at power-up, so the unit followed its Fallback role.
  • Reconnected: the remembered peer was found and the link was re-established.
  • PeerUnreachable: a peer is remembered but did not respond at power-up. The unit works on its own and waits for that peer; it does not search for another one. Boot outcome keeps showing PeerUnreachable as a record of the power-up, even if the peer connects later; the current link state is shown by TWS status.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The units do not pair

  • Roles: one unit must be set to Primary and the other to Secondary. Two Primary units or two Secondary units never pair.
  • Old pairings: neither unit should remember a peer. Check that neither Peer table contains a row marked TWS; if one does, run Start new pairing on that unit.
  • TWS capability: Enable must be selected on both units.
  • Host: switch off Bluetooth on the host during pairing.
  • Distance: place the units close to each other during pairing.
  • Power-up order: switch on the Secondary first and the Primary a few seconds later.
  • Time: allow up to one minute for the units to find each other.

The "Remembered peer did not respond" banner appears. The other unit is switched off, out of range, or no longer has the pairing. If it is switched off or out of range, switch it on or move it closer; the units reconnect automatically and the banner disappears. If the other unit has lost its pairing, or has been reset or replaced, pair the units again: run Start new pairing on both units (one Primary, one Secondary).

Only one unit plays

  • TWS link: on the Bluetooth > TWS page, check TWS status. If it shows Standby, click Reconnect.
  • Input: make sure that the Bluetooth input is selected on the Overview tab of both units.
  • Host: make sure that the host is connected to the Primary.

The host does not reconnect automatically. This is expected when a paired unit is switched on without its peer. Connect manually from the host's Bluetooth settings.

TWS status remains Unsupported while TWS is enabled. Check the Diagnostics group. If Firmware or Device Name shows "---" or n/a, the Bluetooth module is not responding. Power-cycle the unit. If the problem persists, contact MURA LABS support.

All controls in the TWS section are greyed out. TWS capability is set to Disable. Click Enable.

The TWS capability setting is lost after a restart. This is by design: at power-up the unit sets TWS capability automatically. To keep TWS off permanently, forget the peer and set the Fallback role to Standalone (use a unit as a standalone amplifier again).

A button seems to have no effect. Read the status bar at the bottom of the MuraLink window; it explains why most requests are refused. For example, Reconnect reports "already connected" or "No peer is remembered…", and Forget peer can report that the device did not confirm the request. In that case, check the Peer table to see whether the TWS row has been removed.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Pairs only: a unit can be paired with only one peer at a time. Groups of more than two units are not supported.
  • No left/right assignment: both units play the full stereo signal. To play only the left or right channel on a unit, configure the channel routing in its DSP program.
  • One unit per connection: MuraLink connects to one unit at a time over USB, so each unit is configured separately.
  • Lone unit and host: if a paired unit is switched on without its peer, the connection to the host is not restored automatically (Known issues).
  • No host connection during pairing: a unit cannot start TWS pairing while a host is connected to it. Start new pairing disconnects the host automatically.

docs.title: TWS command console
docs.text: The TWS Command Console (expert mode) button opens a separate window that lists every TWS command supported by the firmware. For each command the window provides a send button, a parameter field, and the unit's raw response. The console is intended for development and diagnostics only. Several of its commands change stored settings or drop links without asking for confirmation, so do not use the console for normal setup. Everything described on these pages can be done with the standard controls. The commands themselves are in the command reference.

docs.title: DSP
docs.text:

This section is about programming the ADAU1452 DSP with SigmaStudio: the quick start, the starter project, the boot memory of each board revision, and the parameter interface the firmware uses.

  • Quick start

    SigmaStudio 4.7, the USBi on the I2C-DSP connector, Link Compile Download, and the first checks.

  • The starter project

    What the hierarchy boards do, where to add processing, the ASRCs and the level meter, and the differences between the 1.3 and 1.4 exports.

  • Writing the boot memory

    The memory of each board revision and the SigmaStudio settings that write it; the self-boot check.

  • Boot memory with MuraLink

    Writing the default program or an own E2Prom.Hex from MuraLink on PCB 1.4: the checks, the confirmation, the phases, the optional save of the current program.

  • IPAT and parameters

    How the firmware addresses DSP parameters through the indirect parameter access table, and what a custom design must keep for input selection and the level meter.

docs.title: Boot memory with MuraLink
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.4since 26.10.12026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 ADAU1452 Quick Start, revision 1.1 · 836 kB

On PCB 1.4 the DSP boot memory is an SPI flash the module itself can write, and MuraLink's page DSP > Boot memory does it without SigmaStudio and without the USBi: from the update bundle, which carries the default DSP program, or from your own SigmaStudio self-boot export (E2Prom.Hex). PCB 1.3 modules are programmed through SigmaStudio instead (Writing the boot memory); their page reads Not available on this board.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
• A badge with the availability: Writable, Not available (PCB 1.3), Not supported (firmware before 26.10.1) or n/a; and the memory type, SPI flash.
  • The default program of the opened update bundle for the connected board, with its name, size and the bundle file, or the hint to open a bundle on Device > Firmware update.
  • The check box Save the current DSP program first, off by default: the write then reads the current program into an E2Prom.Hex file you name before it erases anything. Saving a large program takes several minutes. When the flash holds no valid image, nothing is saved and the page says so.
  • The actions Write default from bundle and Write from file..., and during a write the phase and the progress in their place.
DSP > Boot memory.

docs.title: Before a write
docs.text:
• Detach the USBi. While a programmer holds the DSP bus the module does not stay in the power level the write needs, and MuraLink refuses the write.
  • Keep the DSP self boot on (DSP:SELFBOOT? answers 1,1), or the DSP will not load the new program at its next start; MuraLink warns about it.
  • An own export is checked before anything is written: the 0xNN values of the file, the 0xAA sentinel, the block chain, the footer checksum and the size against the 4 MB flash. A failing file is refused with the check named.
  • MuraLink sets the boot read clock of an own export to about 5 MHz and recomputes the footer checksum, and shows the old and the new speed word. SigmaStudio writes another form of the word with the settings of an I2C boot memory, with which the PCB 1.4 boot takes about 3 s instead of 50 ms. The file on disk is not changed. The bundle's image is written as it is.
  • The confirmation names the file, its size and number of blocks and the speed change, and states that the current DSP program is replaced and that the audio stops during the write.

docs.title: The write
docs.text:
MuraLink notes the module's power level, takes it to SLEEP (the DSP in reset frees the flash for the module), and runs the phases Preparing, Saving the current program (if chosen), Erasing, Writing, Verifying and Restarting the DSP with a progress bar. A piece that draws no answer or fails its CRC check is sent again, up to three times; if a knob turn, returning audio, the trigger or a USBi takes the module out of SLEEP, MuraLink sets SLEEP again and repeats the step. The navigation, the device actions and Connect/Disconnect are locked for the duration, and the log records the image source and its SHA-256, every step and the result.

The write succeeds when the CRC-32 of the written range matches the image. MuraLink restores the previous power level; when that restarts the DSP it waits up to 10 s for DSP:BOOT? to report READY and shows the boot time. Written and verified, but the DSP did not start the program means the image or the self-boot setting is wrong, not the write. From SLEEP or STANDBY, or with self boot off, the DSP loads the program at its next start.

A failed write is reported with the step and the module's answer, with the warning that the boot memory may now hold an incomplete program: the DSP does not start and there is no audio until a write succeeds, while the module stays usable and can be written again. MuraLink offers to repeat the write and restores the power level in every case.

docs.title: During a firmware update
docs.text:
When the update bundle carries a DSP image for the connected board, the firmware update asks, before anything is sent, whether to write the default DSP program too. The question shows the image's title, description and changes, and says that the default program replaces whatever the module runs now, an own program included, and that a newer default may contain features an older one did not have. Choose Write the default DSP program or Keep the current DSP program; nothing is preselected, and the choice applies to this update only (Update with MuraLink).

The module keeps no record of which program its boot memory holds (known issue KI-09), so keep your exports with your project, and use Save the current DSP program first when in doubt.

docs.title: Writing the boot memory
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-05Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF guideJP150 ADAU1452 Quick Start, revision 1.1 · 836 kB

The DSP loads its program from a boot memory at every power-up and every wake from sleep or standby. The memory differs between the revisions, and so do the SigmaStudio settings to write it.

PCB 1.4PCB 1.3

A 32 Mbit SPI flash on the DSP's own bus. It can be written in three ways:

  • With MuraLink, from the firmware update bundle (the default program) or from your own SigmaStudio self-boot export (E2Prom.Hex). MuraLink sets the boot read clock and verifies the result. See Boot memory with MuraLink.
  • From SigmaStudio through the DSP (Hardware Configuration, right-click the ADAU1452 block, Self-boot Memory, Write Latest Compilation through DSP) with the settings below.
  • From the control interface with the DSP:FLASH commands, which is what MuraLink uses.

SigmaStudio settings for PCB 1.4:

Parameter Value Protocol SPI Memory size 33554432 bits Page size 256 bytes Number of address bytes 3 Write speed 5000 kHz (this is also the DSP's boot read clock; never below 400 kHz) SPI mode 3 Instructions write enable 06, write 02, read 03, chip erase C7 Chip erase cycle time at least 30 s (60 s for margin)

The self boot does not have to be changed for the write. It is on by default, and it must be on afterwards for the DSP to load the new program. MuraLink shows it on DSP > Status (Self boot); changing it in MuraLink is a future feature. Until then it is changed over the control interface (DSP:SELFBOOT with 1 or 0, wait one second, power cycle).

Warning

With a chip-erase time shorter than the flash needs, SigmaStudio programs the pages while the flash is still erasing; the flash ignores them and stays blank, and the DSP does not boot. SigmaStudio 4.7 does not always keep changed memory settings: check them before every write. An export made with the PCB 1.3 (I2C) settings does not boot on PCB 1.4.

A 512 kbit I2C EEPROM on the DSP's own bus, written from SigmaStudio through the DSP (Hardware Configuration, right-click the ADAU1452 block, Self-boot Memory, Write Latest Compilation through DSP). The position of DIP switch 1 does not matter for the write.

Parameter Value Protocol I2C Memory size 524288 bits Page size 128 bytes Write speed 100 kHz Number of address bytes 2

Never use "Write Latest Compilation USB" on PCB 1.3: it writes over the shared bus to address 0xA0, where the module's settings memory sits. An export made with the PCB 1.4 (SPI) settings does not boot on PCB 1.3.

docs.title: Checking that the program runs
docs.text:
Power the module off, disconnect the USBi, make sure the self boot is on (PCB 1.3: DIP switch 1 OFF; PCB 1.4: the Self boot tile on MuraLink's DSP > Status reading On, or DSP:SELFBOOT? answering 1,1), and power on. On PCB 1.3 do not set DIP switch 1 to ON: that disables the self boot, and a program then runs only from the DSP's RAM and is gone after a power cycle. The green DSP LED flashes at 1 Hz with the default program and audio plays on the selected input. MuraLink's DSP > Status shows the boot outcome and time in the Boot tile and the core state in Core; DSP:BOOT? answers READY with the boot time.

DSP > Status: the *Boot*, *Core* and *Self boot* tiles.

docs.title: IPAT and parameters
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

The firmware does not write into the DSP program's memory by raw address. It goes through the program's indirect parameter access table (IPAT): a table the SigmaStudio design builds, in which each entry names a parameter cell and whether it may be written or read back. The firmware and the hosts address a parameter by its table entry, so a design can change and recompile without the firmware having to know where a cell landed.

docs.title: What the firmware uses
docs.text:
Use Table entry Direction Why it matters Input selection The input mux of the INPUTS_PROCESSING board Write The firmware writes the value of the selected source through it once the DSP program runs, at power-up and after every wake. Without the entry the input cannot be selected and the DSP plays its export default, the test tone Level meter The rms output of the level meter, read-enabled entry 0x600A Read Drives the six LEDs of the level meter, answers DSP:LVLMETER:RMS? and feeds the silence threshold of the automatic power-down. Without it the meter stays dark and the module never powers down on silence

Both come with the starter project. An own design keeps the INPUTS_PROCESSING board unchanged, and with it these two entries and the per-source values of the input mux.

The firmware waits for the DSP program to start before it writes the input, because a parameter written during the boot would be overwritten by the boot image; DSP:BOOT? shows when that happened. The input mux entry is write-only, so the firmware cannot read the selection back; the value SYS:INPUT? reports is the one it last wrote.

docs.title: Your own parameters
docs.text:
A parameter you expose in the table can be written from MuraLink on DSP > Direct memory: under DSP IPAT write, enter the entry's indirect write address as Write address (IPAT) and the Value, and click Write via IPAT; MuraLink asks for a confirmation, because the write affects the live audio path. Over the control interface the same write is DSP:IPAT:SETBLOCK <write_address>,<value>. The write address is the entry's indirect write address from the project's export; the value is the 32-bit word of the cell's format (for example 8.24 fixed point for a gain). Nothing is read back, so a host keeps its own copy of what it wrote. The deprecated DSP:INPUTMUX commands write the mux behind the table instead and are kept only for old software.

DSP > Direct memory: the block write and the write through the IPAT.

DSP:SETBLOCK <address>,<value> (DSP block write on the same MuraLink page) writes a value to a direct DSP address and bypasses the table. It is a diagnostic primitive: a parameter that the table manages must not be written this way, or the program's own copy and the hardware diverge.

How to get started with your first DSP design in SigmaStudio 4.7 on the JP150. The module ships factory-programmed with the starter project shown here, and the same procedure restores the DSP to its factory state.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• SigmaStudio 4.7 from Analog Devices, with its USBi driver (included in the installation; the programmer appears in Device Manager as Analog Devices USBi).
  • The JP150 starter project (Downloads).
  • A JP150 module with its power supply, and a USBi programmer.

docs.title: Hardware setup
docs.text:
1. Self boot. With the self boot enabled the DSP loads its program from the boot memory at power-up. Nothing has to be changed to begin, neither for a download to the running DSP nor for writing the boot memory. PCB 1.3: leave DIP switch 1 OFF; set to ON it disables the self boot, and the DSP runs only the program SigmaStudio downloads into its RAM. PCB 1.4 has no DIP switch: the self boot is a stored setting, enabled by default. MuraLink shows it on DSP > Status (Self boot); changing it in MuraLink is a future feature, until then it is changed with DSP:SELFBOOT over the control interface (Configuration).
  2. Connect the programmer to the I2C-DSP connector (pinout). The module detects it and stands down on that bus (programmer coexistence).

docs.title: Opening and downloading the starter project
docs.text:
1. File, Open, JP150_DSP_basic_passthrough_ASRC.dspproj.
  2. In the Hardware Configuration tab check that the USB block is green: the USBi is connected.
  3. Click Link Compile Download. The status bar reads "Active: Downloaded", and audio applied to the selected input plays.

docs.title: Editing the starter project
docs.text: The main schematic contains the hierarchy boards INPUTS_PROCESSING, AMP0_OUT, AMP1_OUT and I2S_OUT. They abstract the hardware-specific details of the inputs, outputs and sample-rate converters; do not edit them, or the design may stop working with the JP150 firmware. Add your own processing in the marked area of the main schematic. See The starter project.

docs.title: Writing the design into the boot memory
docs.text: Follow Writing the boot memory for your board revision, then power-cycle and check that the DSP LED flashes and audio plays.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom What to check The USB block does not turn green The USB cable; the USBi driver (Device Manager, Analog Devices USBi). A communication error during the download Power the module off, disconnect the USBi from the module and the PC, reconnect the USBi to the PC, power on, reconnect the USBi to the module, download again. After a session the module no longer reacts to input or power changes (PCB 1.4) Reset or power-cycle the module (known issue KI-10). The program does not boot after writing That the self boot is enabled (DIP switch 1 OFF on PCB 1.3; on PCB 1.4 the Self boot tile on MuraLink's DSP > Status reading On, or DSP:SELFBOOT? answering 1,1); the memory settings of the write, in particular the chip-erase time on PCB 1.4; erase, write again, power cycle. MuraLink's DSP > Status (Boot, Core), or DSP:BOOT? and DSP:CORE:STATUS?, tell whether the program loaded.

docs.text:

JP150_DSP_basic_passthrough_ASRC_<version>.dspproj is the SigmaStudio 4.7 project the module ships with: a passthrough of the selected input to both power stages, with the pieces the firmware relies on. Every own design starts from it. The project of the current release is on Downloads; the DSP image of the update bundle for PCB 1.4 is this project's export.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
The main schematic holds four hierarchy boards and a marked area for your own processing:

Board What it does Keep INPUTS_PROCESSING Receives the six sources (I2S, USB, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, S/PDIF, the test tone), brings the asynchronous ones to the DSP's sample rate with sample-rate converters, and selects one of them with the input mux the firmware drives. It also holds the level meter the firmware reads Yes: the firmware's input selection and its level meter depend on the cells and table entries inside (IPAT and parameters) AMP0_OUT, AMP1_OUT Route the stereo signal to the two TAS3251 power stages: left on OUT A, right on OUT B of each stage Yes, unless you redesign the output routing on purpose I2S_OUT Drives the I2S output connector Yes Your processing The area between the input selection and the outputs, marked in the schematic Yours

Everything hardware-specific, the serial ports, the clocking, the sample-rate converters, is inside the boards: do not edit them, or the design may stop working with the firmware. Add your equalisation, crossovers, limiters and routing in the marked area, between the input selection and the output boards.

With the default program the DSP LED flashes at 1 Hz (on PCB 1.4 it is driven by the DSP's MP7 pin), which is how you see that a program runs after a download or a boot-memory write.

docs.title: One design, two boards
docs.text: The design is the same on PCB 1.3 and 1.4; the self-boot memory differs. The project stores the memory settings of one board at a time, so an export made with the settings of the other board does not boot (Writing the boot memory). The project of a release carries the PCB 1.4 settings; set the PCB 1.3 values before a write to a PCB 1.3 module and check them before every write, because SigmaStudio 4.7 does not always keep changed memory settings.

docs.title: Working with it
docs.text:
1. Open the project, check the USBi in the Hardware Configuration tab, and Link Compile Download to try a change on the running DSP (Quick start).
  2. When the design is right, write it into the boot memory: on PCB 1.4 from MuraLink with the project's E2Prom.Hex export (Boot memory with MuraLink) or through the DSP from SigmaStudio; on PCB 1.3 through the DSP from SigmaStudio.
  3. Keep the exported files with your project: the module has no record of which program its boot memory holds (known issue KI-09).

Three things are configured on the board itself: the DSP boot source, the MCU boot mode and the output bridging. PCB 1.3 uses a DIP switch for the first two; PCB 1.4 has no DIP switch and keeps them in firmware settings and a factory jumper.

docs.title: DSP boot and MCU boot
docs.text:
PCB 1.4PCB 1.3

PCB 1.4 has no configuration DIP switch. since 26.10.1

Function Where it lives on PCB 1.4 DSP self boot from the boot memory A stored firmware setting, on by default. MuraLink shows it on DSP > Status (Self boot); changing it in MuraLink is a future feature. Until then it is changed over the control interface, DSP:SELFBOOT with 1 or 0, and acts at the next DSP reset, so a power cycle follows a change. With the self boot off there is no audio. Master clock source Selected by the firmware. The current firmware always selects the internal clock. MCU boot mode The ST ROM bootloader is reachable only through a factory solder jumper (STM BOOT) and is unavailable on production modules. Firmware updates and recovery go through the module's own update mode: Firmware updates.

A three-position DIP switch next to the DSP.

Switch Function ON OFF 1 DSP EEPROM BOOT Self boot disabled: the DSP runs only a program downloaded from SigmaStudio into its RAM Self boot enabled, the normal position: the DSP loads its program from the on-board EEPROM at power-up 2 INTERNAL MCLK Internal master clock No effect in the current firmware: the module always runs from its internal clock 3 MCU BOOT MODE ST ROM bootloader Normal operation

Switch 3 from firmware 26.10.1

A PCB 1.3 module that runs firmware 26.10.1 or later must keep switch 3 OFF for good. The old updater cannot talk to such a module, and a wrong move can erase it. Updates come through MuraLink: Update with MuraLink.

The firmware also stores a DSP self-boot setting (DSP:SELFBOOT, on by default); switch 1 set to ON keeps the self boot off whatever the setting says.

docs.title: Output bridging (BTL and PBTL)
docs.text: Each TAS3251 drives two channels in BTL, or one channel in PBTL with double the current. The bridging is set with three solder jumpers per power stage (silkscreen: BTL = open, PBTL = closed, all three alike), on both revisions. The DSP program must match: a PBTL stage expects one channel.

docs.title: Reset button
docs.text: The push button marked STM RST resets the host MCU and its peripherals. Settings are kept; the module starts as after a power cycle.

docs.title: Connectors and pinouts
docs.text:

On this page you find the pinout of every connector, under the name printed next to it on the board. Pick your board revision once, in the tabs below or in the filter at the top of the page; every tab on the site follows the choice. Pin 1 is the pin marked on the board next to each connector.

PCB 1.3 from the connector side, with the names used on this page.

To be added

Drawings of the connector positions of PCB 1.3 and PCB 1.4, which differ slightly.

Check the revision before you make a cable

PCB 1.4 moved the pins of the I2S, UART1, DSP GPIO and 5 V connectors. A cable made for a 1.3 board fits a 1.4 board mechanically, with the signals in other positions. Read the revision from the silkscreen, or ask the module: SYS:BOARD:TYPE? answers JP150-1.3 or JP150-1.4.

docs.title: Power inputs
docs.text:
DC-IN (POWER IN). Screw terminal, 15 to 36 V DC: pin 1 GND, pin 2 positive. The module has reverse-polarity protection and soft-start inrush limiting. Keep the supply leads short and low-impedance; do not exceed 36 V (see Specifications).

USB-PD (USB C PD). USB Power Delivery input up to 100 W, power only. On PCB 1.4 a green LED next to the connector shows that a USB-C source is present, and the firmware reports it (SYS:POWER:USBC?).

docs.title: Speaker outputs
docs.text: Four screw-terminal outputs for the two TAS3251 power stages: AMP0 OUT A, AMP0 OUT B, AMP1 OUT A, AMP1 OUT B, each with its + and − pin marked. With the default DSP program, OUT A carries the left and OUT B the right channel of each power stage; an own DSP program can route the channels differently. The BTL and PBTL bridging options are on Configuration.

docs.title: I2S input and output
docs.text:
PCB 1.4PCB 1.3

JST PH, 5 pins. Two connectors as before (I2S INPUT, I2S OUTPUT) plus the auxiliary output (I2S OUTPUT AUX) on the DSP's serial output port 1. since 26.10.1

Pin I2S INPUT I2S OUTPUT I2S OUTPUT AUX 1 GND GND GND 2 BCLK BCLK BCLK 1 3 GND GND GND 4 LRCLK LRCLK LRCLK 1 5 DATA IN DATA OUT DATA OUT 1

JST PH, 5 pins. Two connectors (I2S INPUT, I2S OUTPUT); PCB 1.3 has no auxiliary output.

Pin I2S INPUT I2S OUTPUT 1 DATA IN DATA OUT 2 GND GND 3 BCLK BCLK 4 GND GND 5 LRCLK LRCLK

Use shielded cable for the best signal integrity. Digital audio up to 96 kHz / 32 bit, I2S and TDM modes, as configured in the DSP program.

docs.title: User UART (UART1)
docs.text:
PCB 1.4PCB 1.3 Pin Signal Description 1 GND Ground reference 2 TX UART transmit from the module 3 RX UART receive into the module, 5 V tolerant Pin Signal Description 1 RX UART receive into the module, 5 V tolerant 2 TX UART transmit from the module 3 GND Ground reference

115200 bit/s, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, 3.3 V logic. Connect the module to a host with a common ground and crossed lines (host TX to module RX). The same command set is available on the USB virtual COM port; see Control interface.

docs.title: Slave UART (UART SLAVE)
docs.text: JST PH, 3 pins, the same on both revisions: pin 1 TX (from the module), pin 2 RX, pin 3 GND. For connecting another module.

docs.title: DSP I2C (I2C-DSP)
docs.text:
JST PH, 3 pins, the same on both revisions: pin 1 SDA, pin 2 SCL, pin 3 GND. The connector for the SigmaStudio USBi programmer.

PCB 1.4PCB 1.3

A bus the DSP has to itself (the module's own control bus for the DSP, 400 kHz). The power stages, the temperature sensor, the settings memory and the supply monitor are on another bus. The programmer coexistence rules still apply: a connected USBi suspends the module's own DSP traffic.

The module's shared system bus: the DSP, both power stages, the settings memory and the temperature sensor share it. A SigmaStudio session therefore shares the bus with the amplifier control, which the firmware arbitrates (programmer coexistence). Never use SigmaStudio's "Write Latest Compilation USB" on PCB 1.3: it writes to I2C address 0xA0, where the module's settings memory sits.

docs.title: User I2C and DSP GPIO
docs.text:
PCB 1.4PCB 1.3

On PCB 1.4 the connector carries two multipurpose pins of the ADAU1452 (silkscreen DSP GPIO): pin 1 MP6, pin 2 MP7, pin 3 GND. MP7 also drives the DSP status LED. Their function is defined by the DSP program; the firmware does not use them.

Reserved for future firmware (silkscreen I2C-USER): pin 1 SDA, pin 2 SCL, pin 3 GND, on a separate I2C bus of the MCU. Not used by the current firmware.

docs.title: DSP GPIO / ADC inputs (DSP ADC)
docs.text:
Auxiliary ADC and GPIO inputs of the ADAU1452, JST PH, 8 pins.

PCB 1.4PCB 1.3 Pin Signal 1 GND 2 ADC5 3 ADC4 4 ADC3 5 ADC2 6 ADC1 7 ADC0 8 3V3 Pin Signal 1 3V3 2 ADC0 3 ADC1 4 ADC2 5 ADC3 6 ADC4 7 ADC5 8 GND

docs.title: Encoder (ROTARY ENCODER)
docs.text:
JST PH, 4 pins, the same on both revisions.

Pin Signal Description 1 ENC_A Quadrature signal A 2 ENC_SW Encoder push button 3 ENC_B Quadrature signal B 4 GND Ground reference

Rotate to change the volume, press to cycle the inputs. Holding the button while switching the module on enters the bootloader's update mode (Recovery). The encoder is optional; the module is fully controllable over UART and USB.

docs.title: 12 V trigger (12V TRIGGER)
docs.text:
PCB 1.4 only

JST PH, 2 pins: pin 1 trigger input, pin 2 GND. A 3.3 V to 12 V signal reads as active; the input has a series resistor and a 3.3 V clamp. What the module does with it is set by the trigger mode, see 12 V trigger. since 26.10.1

docs.title: 5 V output (5V PSU)
docs.text:
JST PH, 2 pins. 5 V from the module's own regulator for an external control board; switched off in standby.

PCB 1.4PCB 1.3 Pin Signal 1 +5 V 2 GND Pin Signal 1 GND 2 +5 V

docs.title: USB data (USB DATA)
docs.text:
Use either the USB-C receptacle or the 3-pin JST header, both labelled USB DATA, for USB data. The module enumerates as one composite device: USB Audio and a virtual COM port carrying the control command set. From firmware 26.10.1 the device identifies as 16D0:15B8 ("MURA LABS JP150"); the bootloader's update mode as 16D0:15B7. Firmware 26.8.0 and earlier identified as 0483:5741.

Pin (3-pin header) Signal 1 USB D− 2 USB D+ 3 GND

docs.title: Neopixel (NEOPIXEL)
docs.text: JST PH, 3 pins, the same on both revisions: pin 1 GND, pin 2 DATA, pin 3 3V3 OUT. Reserved for an external addressable LED chain; the on-board indicators are on the same data line.

docs.text: Connector Function MCLK-IN External master clock input. Not used by the current firmware (the module runs from its internal clock). MCLK-OUT DSP clock output (buffered on PCB 1.4). docs.text:

The module has a power LED, a status LED, a DSP LED and a six-LED level meter on both revisions. PCB 1.4 adds indicators for the power stages, the Bluetooth module and the USB-C supply.

PCB 1.3: the status and power LEDs, the level meter, the reset button and the Neopixel connector sit along the edge next to the speaker terminals.

docs.title: Main indicators
docs.text: Element Function Behaviour Power LED Power and firmware heartbeat A low level with a short bright blip once per second while the firmware runs. In any power-down level it goes dark with a short flash every two seconds. Status LED Input and state Input colours: blue Bluetooth, white Wi-Fi, magenta USB, cyan I2S, amber S/PDIF, yellow internal 1 kHz sine. Bluetooth and TWS patterns: LED reference. Off in any power-down level, restored on waking. DSP LED DSP activity Flashing means the DSP program runs (1 Hz with the default program). Dark in sleep and standby, where the DSP is held in reset. On PCB 1.4 it is driven by the DSP's MP7 pin. Level meter Signal level of the selected input, ahead of the volume control Cleared in any power-down level; frozen on its last reading while a SigmaStudio programmer is active.

docs.title: Special patterns
docs.text:
State Status LED Level meter Unsupported board, safe state since 26.10.1 Red with a dim white step every second Dark Fatal error Red blink – Update mode and firmware installation Amber patterns, blue progress, green or red result: see LED indication during updates Progress bar in blue

The safe state means the firmware found no factory record it supports on the board (a bare development board, or a record of another product). The outputs stay muted and only the identification and update commands answer; see Start-up and the safe state.

docs.text:
Silkscreen Colour Meaning AMP0 CLIP, AMP1 CLIP Yellow The power stage reports clipping. AMP0 FAULT, AMP1 FAULT Red The power stage reports a fault (over-temperature, over-current or under-voltage). The decoded fault is readable with AMP0:FAULT? / AMP1:FAULT?. BT LED Blue, green The Bluetooth module's own status LEDs. USB C PD Green A USB-C power source is connected.

The power-stage and Bluetooth indicators can be disabled by removing the 0 Ω links marked AMP LED DISABLE and BT LED DISABLE.

docs.text: On part of the first PCB 1.4 production batch the power LED, status LED and level meter show white or random colours after power-on. Audio and control are not affected; a firmware fix is in preparation. See Known issues.

docs.title: Power levels and consumption
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

The module operates in one of five power levels. Each switches off progressively more; the control interface (UART and USB) answers at every level, including standby.

Level Power stage DSP Wi-Fi module Idle current at 36 V (PCB 1.3) NORMAL Playing Running Powered 250 mA PWRSTAGE_IDLE Muted Running Powered 120 mA PWRSTAGE_OFF Muted, unpowered Running Powered 75 mA SLEEP Muted, unpowered Stopped Powered 55 mA STANDBY Muted, unpowered Stopped Unpowered 30 mA

The currents are typical measured values on PCB 1.3 with no audio playing. They depend on the DSP program, the Wi-Fi module's network activity and the Bluetooth connection state.

To be added

The idle currents of PCB 1.4 at 36 V, as a second column of the table.

docs.title: Entering and leaving a level
docs.text:
Levels are entered from MuraLink or by command, by automatic power-down, or on PCB 1.4 by the 12 V trigger. SLEEP keeps the Wi-Fi module powered, so the module stays reachable on the network and wakes when you play to it; STANDBY is the only level that removes Wi-Fi power.

Returning from a level that removed power from the power stages takes several hundred milliseconds, because the power stages are re-initialised. Waking from SLEEP or STANDBY also restarts the DSP, which reloads its program from the boot memory: about 50 ms on PCB 1.4, 200 to 250 ms on PCB 1.3. Audio is back within about a second.

In STANDBY the host MCU keeps running and answering commands, which accounts for most of the remaining current.

docs.title: In MuraLink
docs.text:
Device > Power Modes: the Power mode row has a button per level (Normal, PS idle, PS off, Sleep, Standby); the current level is highlighted and a click switches at once. The automatic power-down and, on PCB 1.4, the 12 V trigger are set on the same page.

Device > Power Modes: the power level, the automatic power-down and, on PCB 1.4, the 12 V trigger.

docs.title: Over the control interface
docs.text: SYS:POWER:MODE? answers the level and SYS:POWER:MODE with a level name of the table above sets it; the control interface answers at every level (SYS:POWER reference).

docs.title: Safety, handling and notes
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

  • High-power outputs. Make sure the speaker wiring is secure and insulated. Disconnect the power before servicing.
  • Supply voltage. 15 to 36 V DC. Do not exceed 36 V: the power stages and, on PCB 1.4, the supply monitor are specified to that limit.
  • Thermal design. Full-power operation needs adequate airflow and a properly mounted heatsink. Observe the operating temperature range of −10 to +60 °C.
  • EMI and EMC. Keep speaker leads twisted and short. Use shielded cables for S/PDIF and USB where applicable.
  • ESD. Handle the module with standard ESD precautions.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• Two TAS3251 Class-D power stages: 4 × 150 W, 2 × 300 W or 2.1 configurations.
  • Typical distortion 0.005 % THD+N at 10 W into 4 Ω and 0.015 % at 100 W into 4 Ω (1 kHz).
  • ADAU1452 SigmaDSP, programmable in SigmaStudio, for EQ, crossovers, dynamics and routing.
  • Digital inputs up to 96 kHz / 32 bit: I2S and TDM, S/PDIF, USB, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi.
  • Wi-Fi streaming with the on-board LinkPlay A31 module: AirPlay, Spotify Connect, DLNA and UPnP (Wi-Fi).
  • Streaming services through the 4STREAM app, among them Spotify, TIDAL, Qobuz, Amazon Music, SoundCloud, TuneIn, iHeartRadio, Napster and internet radio; music files from a phone, a PC or a NAS on the local network.
  • Wi-Fi multiroom: several modules play in sync as a group or each its own source.
  • True Wireless Stereo over Bluetooth, with a remembered partner (TWS).
  • Control over UART and USB (virtual COM port) with one command set; MuraLink on Windows.
  • Dual power input with automatic selection: DC 15 to 36 V and USB Power Delivery up to 100 W.
  • Firmware updates from the PC with MuraLink, installed by the module's own bootloader. since 26.10.1
  • Automatic power-down with wake on audio, per-input enable, SigmaStudio programmer coexistence.
  • Supply voltage, current and power, MCU and power-stage temperature, per-stage clip, fault and clock reporting.
  • PCB 1.4: 12 V trigger input, USB-C power sensing, a second I2S output, DSP boot memory written from the PC, per-stage clip and fault LEDs.

docs.title: Typical applications
docs.text:
• Active loudspeakers (two- or three-way) with on-board crossovers and equalisation.
  • 2.1 and four-channel amplifiers for portable or installed audio.
  • Network audio receivers with DSP and high-power amplification.
  • A development platform for ADAU1452 SigmaStudio projects with a high-power output stage.

docs.title: Functional blocks
docs.text:
To be added

A block diagram of the module's internal architecture.

  • Audio inputs and outputs. I2S/TDM input and output headers (PCB 1.4 adds a second output), S/PDIF in and out, USB audio, the Bluetooth module and the Wi-Fi module.
  • DSP. The ADAU1452 SigmaDSP with its boot memory, an I2C EEPROM on PCB 1.3 and an SPI flash on PCB 1.4, and the SigmaStudio programmer connector (DSP).
  • Power amplification. Two TAS3251 devices driving four channels in BTL, or configurable for PBTL and 2.1 (Configuration).
  • Control and monitoring. The STM32 host microcontroller with its bootloader and the factory record in its OTP memory; input selection and enabling, DSP control, the power levels with automatic power-down and, on PCB 1.4, the 12 V trigger; the programmer detection, the settings memory, the watchdog, and the monitoring of supply, temperatures and power stages (an INA226 power monitor on PCB 1.4).
  • User interface. The encoder, the status, power and DSP LEDs and the level meter; on PCB 1.3 the configuration DIP switch, on PCB 1.4 the clip, fault, Bluetooth and USB-C indicators (Indicators and LEDs).
  • Power. DC-IN 15 to 36 V and USB-PD up to 100 W with automatic selection, reverse-polarity protection and inrush limiting; a 5 V output for accessories.

docs.title: MuraLink
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

MuraLink is the Windows application for the module. This section covers its installation, its pages, and the firmware releases it supports.

  • Install

    System requirements, download, first start, connecting a module.

  • Pages reference

    Every MuraLink page with what it shows and does.

  • Firmware compatibility

    Which MuraLink version works with which firmware release, and what shows n/a on older firmware.

docs.title: Firmware compatibility
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

MuraLink is released together with the firmware and carries the same version scheme. One rule makes the combinations work: MuraLink makes no version check, it tries each command and treats a command that draws no answer three times in a row (while ping still answers) as not implemented on this connection. The value then reads n/a, the control is greyed with the tooltip Not supported by the connected firmware, and the command is not sent again until the next connection or a manual refresh. Every page keeps working around the gaps.

docs.title: Which MuraLink for which firmware
docs.text:
Use the MuraLink of the firmware release or a newer one. MuraLink 26.10.1 works with every firmware from 26.6.2 on; the older the firmware, the more reads n/a:

Firmware What MuraLink 26.10.1 cannot show or do 26.10.1 Nothing: every page is live 26.8.0 The start-up diagnostics (reset cause, bootloader information, settings-memory state, kernel figures); the TWS management (the TWS page is greyed, the fallback role, the peer memory); the board type and everything of PCB 1.4; the autosave indicator and Reset settings; the update bundle: the first update is arranged with support 26.7.0 As 26.8.0, and the input enable switches, the programmer detection, the automatic power-down settings and its countdown 26.6.2 As 26.7.0, and the level meter, the fault decoding and the per-stage reset controls, the board identity, the IPAT write. Settings are kept in flash only: Device > Status offers Save to flash instead of the autosave line

A firmware newer than MuraLink works too, with its new features invisible, with one exception: MuraLink 26.8.0 and older poll a DSP command that 26.10.1 removed, so their DSP page stops updating, and they have no firmware update page. With firmware 26.10.1 use MuraLink 26.10.1 or newer.

docs.title: Boards
docs.text: MuraLink reads the board type on connect (SYS:BOARD:TYPE?). On a board the firmware does not support it shows a banner, keeps the identification and the firmware update available and limits its polling to the reduced command set of the safe state. On PCB 1.3 the controls of PCB 1.4 features (the 12 V trigger, the USB-C power sense, the DSP boot memory page) are greyed with the tooltip Not available on this board.

docs.title: Firmware updates
docs.text: The firmware update page installs an update bundle on a module that runs 26.10.1 or newer, and on a module that waits in update mode without a firmware. A PCB 1.3 module on 26.8.0 or older cannot take an update bundle by itself; MuraLink names that case as Secure bootloader missing, and the first update is arranged with support.

docs.title: Settings persistence
docs.text: How a module keeps its settings depends on its firmware, and MuraLink shows it on Device > Status: Saved automatically from 26.7.0 on (the autosave), with the footer indicator and Reset settings from 26.10.1 on; on 26.6.2 Save to flash writes the volumes, the input and the Bluetooth role to the flash record, and the other settings return to their defaults at every start of such a unit.

docs.title: Install MuraLink
docs.text: JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit.
  • A free USB port and a USB-C data cable for the module's USB DATA connector, or a serial adapter on its UART1 connector (115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit).

Nothing has to be installed first. Everything MuraLink needs, the .NET runtime included, is inside its executable.

docs.title: Download and first start
docs.text:
1. Download MuraLink_26.10.1.zip from Downloads. It is a zip of about 67 MB with no installer and no registry entries. It holds the executable MuraLink_26.10.1.exe (about 165 MB), a README.txt and the licence files of the embedded fonts and icons.
  2. Unzip it into a folder you can write to, for example under Documents. MuraLink writes its log files into a Logs folder next to the executable (dsp-amp-YYYYMMDD.log); a copy of the current log is the first thing support asks for.
  3. Start MuraLink_26.10.1.exe. Windows SmartScreen may warn about a program downloaded for the first time; choose More info and Run anyway. The first start unpacks the application's native libraries into %TEMP%\.net\MuraLink_26.10.1. The application version is shown in the footer of the window.

To update MuraLink, unzip the new package into a folder of its own, or replace the executable with the new one; nothing else is stored on the PC apart from the logs and the unpacked libraries under %TEMP%.

docs.title: Connecting a module
docs.text:
1. Connect the module to the PC with a USB-C data cable on USB DATA (the USB-C connector or the 3-pin header). Windows needs no driver: the module enumerates as a USB audio device and a COM port (USB 16D0:15B8 from firmware 26.10.1, 0483:5741 before). Charge-only cables carry no data.
  2. In MuraLink open the connection dialog (the connection pill at the top right), choose the COM port of the module and click Connect. The serial settings matter only for a UART connection; over USB any baud rate works.
  3. MuraLink reads the module's identity and its state and shows the Overview. The connection pill reads JP150 connected.
The Device connection dialog behind the connection pill.

What MuraLink shows when the firmware is older than itself, and what it cannot do on an unsupported board, is on Firmware compatibility. The Pages reference walks through the window.

docs.title: Pages reference
docs.text:

MuraLink's window has a sidebar with seven sections; most sections have sub-tabs. The connection pill at the top right opens the connection dialog in every state, and the footer shows the last action's result, the autosave indicator (Saving..., Settings saved) and the application version. A value the connected firmware cannot report reads n/a (Firmware compatibility).

The Overview: the input tiles, the volume and the device health.

docs.title: Automatic power-down
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.8.02026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

The module can watch its selected input for silence and drop to a lower power level after a configurable period, returning to normal when audio comes back. The feature is disabled by default.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Range Default Enable on, off off Target level any level except NORMAL PWRSTAGE_OFF Delay 10 to 65535 s (about 18 h) 1800 s (30 min) Silence threshold raw level-meter units 5

Silence is measured at the source, ahead of the volume control. A muted power stage that is still fed audio does not power down; paused audio counts as silence, so a paused source eventually powers the module down. The default threshold treats only near-digital silence as silent; a source with a residual DC offset or dither may never let the module power down, in which case raise the threshold.

docs.title: In MuraLink
docs.text:
Device > Power Modes, section Automatic power-down: the Automatic power mode switch enables or disables the feature and applies at once. Power down to chooses the target level, After silence of the delay in minutes and seconds, and Silence threshold the level below which the input counts as silent (0 would never be silent); Apply power-mode settings sends the three values to the module. While the timer runs, the page shows the countdown.

Device > Power Modes: the power level, the automatic power-down and, on PCB 1.4, the 12 V trigger.

docs.title: Over the control interface
docs.text:
Setting Commands Enable SYS:POWER:AUTO?, SYS:POWER:AUTO with 0 or 1 Target level SYS:POWER:AUTO:MODE?, SYS:POWER:AUTO:MODE with the level Delay SYS:POWER:AUTO:DELAY?, SYS:POWER:AUTO:DELAY with the seconds Silence threshold SYS:POWER:AUTO:THRESHOLD?, SYS:POWER:AUTO:THRESHOLD with the raw value

SYS:POWER:AUTO:STATE? returns the enable state, whether the timer runs, the configured and the effective target, the delay and the elapsed and remaining seconds, so a host can show a countdown. The syntax and the answers are in the SYS:POWER reference.

docs.title: Wake sources
docs.text: The module returns to normal operation on an encoder turn or press, on audio returning on the selected input, on a SigmaStudio programmer appearing on the DSP bus, and on any reset. The encoder action that wakes the module only wakes it: it does not also change the volume or the input, which you cannot see while powered down. On PCB 1.4 the 12 V trigger can wake the module as well.

docs.title: Target level clamping by input
docs.text:
The module limits itself to a level it can reliably wake from, which depends on the selected input.

Selected input Deepest level entered Reason USB STANDBY Incoming USB audio is detected by the host MCU directly. Bluetooth STANDBY The Bluetooth module reports the playback state. Wi-Fi SLEEP STANDBY would remove power from the Wi-Fi module. S/PDIF, I2S PWRSTAGE_OFF Only the DSP sees these signals, so it must keep running. Sine generator never powers down The internal generator is never silent.

A configured target deeper than the clamp is silently reduced; both the configured and the effective target are readable. USB caveat: powered down, the module sees USB packets arriving but not their content, so a computer that streams digital silence rather than stopping its stream reads as active and wakes the module about once per delay. Select another input, or leave automatic power-down off, with such a host.

Automatic power-down is suspended while a SigmaStudio programmer is active, and, with the trigger priority set, while the 12 V trigger holds the module awake.

docs.title: Inputs and the enable mask
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

The module has six audio sources: USB, Bluetooth, S/PDIF, I2S, Wi-Fi and an internal 1 kHz sine generator for tests. One source is active at a time, selected with the encoder button, in MuraLink or over the control interface. The status LED shows the selected source by colour (Indicators).

docs.title: Enabling and disabling sources
docs.text:
Each source can be enabled or disabled individually. A disabled source is skipped when cycling with the encoder and refused when it is selected from MuraLink or over the control interface. Two rules apply:

  • At least one source always stays enabled; disabling the last one is refused.
  • Disabling the active source moves the module to the next enabled one.

The enable mask is stored and survives a power cycle; all six sources are enabled by default and after a settings reset.

docs.title: Selection and the DSP
docs.text:
The selected input is routed inside the DSP program. The firmware sends the selection to the DSP once the program runs, at power-up and after every wake from SLEEP or STANDBY, so the selection is kept across power levels. since 26.10.1

The selected input is one of the settings that a settings reset keeps (Settings and memory).

docs.title: In MuraLink
docs.text:
The Overview shows the six sources as tiles under Audio input, the active one highlighted; click a tile to select that source. Configure inputs opens the Inputs page with a check box per source under Available inputs: clear a box to disable the source, tick it to enable it again. The two rules above apply, and the footer shows the result of a change. The Overview also shows the level of the selected input.

The Overview: click a tile to select the source. The Inputs page behind *Configure inputs*: a switch per source.

SYS:INPUT:<source> Select a source SYS:INPUT with the source SYS:INPUT:OK, or ERR:DISABLED for a disabled source Read whether a source is enabled SYS:INPUT:ENABLE? with the source SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:<source>:<0|1> Enable or disable a source SYS:INPUT:ENABLE with the source and 0 or 1 SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:OK, or ERR:LAST when it would disable the last enabled source List the enabled sources SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:LIST? The source names, the exact syntax and the answers are in the SYS:INPUT reference; what a host must handle is on Integration notes.
