More than one JP150 can play in one system. Three ways exist, each with its own place on this site.

docs.title: Audio over I2S
docs.text:
Feed the audio into the first module through I2S INPUT and forward it to the next module through I2S OUTPUT; the next module's I2S INPUT takes it, and so on. What the output carries is decided by the DSP program: the default program forwards the selected input, so a chain plays the same signal everywhere, and an own program can send a processed or a different signal down the chain (for example the subwoofer feed of a 2.1 system). PCB 1.4 has a second output, I2S OUTPUT AUX, driven by the DSP's second serial port, which an own program can use for a second chain or a different mix. Pinouts and the pin-order differences between the revisions are on Connectors and pinouts; the DSP side is on The starter project.

Clocking, channel mapping and synchronisation along the chain are decided in the DSP programs of the modules; the firmware does not configure them.

docs.title: Audio over the network
docs.text: Several modules on the same network each receive their own stream from the streaming apps (Wi-Fi setup); grouping and synchronisation are done by the apps and the Wi-Fi module, not by the firmware. In the 4STREAM app several modules can be grouped to play in sync, or each plays its own source (what the Wi-Fi module can do). The module's volume follows the app's volume during playback (Volume and encoder).

docs.title: Two modules over Bluetooth
docs.text: A pair of modules plays one phone's audio in sync as a True Wireless Stereo pair: the phone connects to the Primary, which forwards the audio to the Secondary. Both play the full stereo signal; a left/right split is made in the DSP program. The whole procedure is in the Bluetooth section.

docs.title: Control
docs.text: Every module has its own control interface over USB and UART1, and MuraLink connects to one module at a time; a host that controls several modules opens one connection per module. The UART SLAVE connector is provided for connecting another module.

docs.title: SigmaStudio programmer coexistence
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.8.02026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

A SigmaStudio USBi programmer on the DSP I2C connector is a second master on the bus the firmware uses to talk to the DSP. The firmware detects it within milliseconds and stands down until it has finished, so a DSP download or live tuning can be done on a running module without any preparation.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The firmware samples the bus lines at 10 kHz and, on traffic it did not originate, suspends its own periodic DSP access for 750 ms after the last foreign transaction, re-arming as long as the programmer remains active. While a programmer is active:

  • the level meter freezes on its last reading, because the firmware is not reading the DSP;
  • automatic power-down is suspended, so a tuning session is never interrupted;
  • mute, reset and fault clearing stay available.

A bus held low for more than 3 s is reported separately as a stuck bus (a wiring or hardware fault), and the programmer indication is cleared while a stuck bus is present. MuraLink shows External programmer in the strip above its DSP pages while one is active and greys out the controls that use the bus; over the control interface the read-only queries SYS:I2C:GUARD?, SYS:I2C:GUARD:COUNT? and SYS:I2C:GUARD:STUCK? report the state, the number of episodes and a stuck bus (SYS:I2C:GUARD reference).

docs.title: Which bus
docs.text:
PCB 1.4PCB 1.3

The DSP has its own bus. The programmer never shares a bus with the power stages, the temperature sensor or the settings memory, so volume changes and measurements continue during a session.

The DSP shares the system bus with the power stages, the temperature sensor and the settings memory. During a session the firmware's own traffic on that bus pauses.

docs.title: Known issue
docs.text: After a SigmaStudio session on PCB 1.4 the guard can stay active until the module is reset, even with the USBi unplugged; DSP queries then answer ERROR and input or power-mode changes do not reach the DSP. Reset or power-cycle the module after using the USBi. See Known issues.

docs.title: Settings and memory
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

This page explains what the module remembers across a power cycle, when it writes it, how you return it to the defaults, and what an update does with it.

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text:
Setting Default Set with Kept by a settings reset Master volume and the volume of each power stage – Encoder, MuraLink, AMP:VOL, AMP0:VOL, AMP1:VOL No Selected input – Encoder button, MuraLink, SYS:INPUT Yes Input enable mask All six enabled MuraLink Configure inputs, SYS:INPUT:ENABLE No Automatic power-down: enable, target level, delay, threshold Off, PWRSTAGE_OFF, 1800 s, 5 MuraLink Device > Power Modes, SYS:POWER:AUTO and its :MODE, :DELAY, :THRESHOLD No DSP self boot On DSP:SELFBOOT No 12 V trigger: mode, target, priority (PCB 1.4) OFF, SLEEP, 1 MuraLink Device > Power Modes, SYS:TRIG:MODE, :TARGET, :PRIORITY No TWS fallback role Primary MuraLink Bluetooth > TWS, BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE Yes Board identity The factory record Factory Yes

Three more things survive a power cycle but live elsewhere and are not touched by a settings reset: the Bluetooth name and the Bluetooth pairings (in the Bluetooth module), the Wi-Fi network (in the Wi-Fi module) and the DSP program (in the DSP's boot memory).

docs.title: When a setting is written
docs.text:
The firmware writes a setting to the settings memory once it has stayed unchanged for a moment, so that a turn of the encoder is not written at every step:

Settings Written after DSP self boot, the trigger settings 0.1 s Input enable mask, TWS fallback role 1 s Selected input 2 s Volumes 3 s Automatic power-down settings 5 s

MuraLink's footer shows Saving... until the write is done and then Settings saved; SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING? answers 1 while a write is outstanding. A restart (*RST), the entry into update mode and the settings reset write pending changes first, so a change made right before them is not lost. since 26.10.1

At start the firmware reports how the settings memory came up (SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE?; MuraLink shows it on Device > Status): OK means the settings were restored; NODATA means the memory was empty or held an older layout, the defaults and the backup copy are in use and the autosave fills it; ABSENT or ERROR means a fault, and nothing is saved in that session.

docs.title: Reset to the defaults
docs.text:
A settings reset returns the settings marked "No" in the table above to their defaults and restarts the module: the volumes, the enable mask, the automatic power-down, the DSP self boot and the trigger settings. The selected input, the TWS fallback role and the board identity stay, and so do the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi pairings and the DSP program. The outputs are muted until the module has restarted, which takes a few seconds. since 26.10.1

  • In MuraLink: Device > Status, Reset settings under Service actions, and confirm.
  • Over the control interface: SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS, answered with SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS:OK before the restart (SYS:NVM reference).
Device > Status: *Reset settings* under the service actions.

docs.title: Settings across updates
docs.text: A firmware update keeps the settings. The first start of 26.10.1 after 26.8.0 is the one exception: the settings memory changed its layout, and the stored settings are rebuilt once. The input enable mask, the automatic power-down and the then new settings (self boot, trigger) start from their defaults; the volumes, the selected input and the TWS fallback role are kept. SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE? answers NODATA on that first start and OK from the next one.

docs.title: Older firmware
docs.text: Firmware 26.6.2 kept the volumes, the input and the Bluetooth role in flash only, written by a command; MuraLink offers Save to flash on such a module. From 26.7.0 on the settings memory and the autosave described here are in use (Firmware compatibility).

docs.title: Start-up and the safe state
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.10.12026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

docs.title: What happens at power-up
docs.text:
1. The bootloader verifies the installed firmware and starts it. A firmware that fails the check is never started; the module waits in update mode instead (Recovery).
  2. The firmware reads the board's factory record and configures itself for PCB 1.3 or 1.4.
  3. The LEDs, the encoder and the control interface respond immediately. The firmware no longer waits for the DSP before anything else runs, so the level meter shows no random colours at power-up.
  4. The DSP loads its program from the boot memory: about 50 ms on PCB 1.4 (SPI flash), 200 to 250 ms on PCB 1.3 (I2C EEPROM). Audio starts when the program runs; the selected input is sent to the DSP at that moment. MuraLink shows the outcome and the time on DSP > Status (Boot); DSP:BOOT? reports them.
  5. The stored settings are applied: volume, input, enable mask, automatic power-down, trigger and DSP self boot.

A watchdog supervises every firmware task. A module that stops responding restarts itself instead of staying silent; MuraLink's Diagnostics > System then names the watchdog as the cause of the last reset, and SYS:RESET:CAUSE? answers IWDG.

docs.title: Board identity
docs.text: Every provisioned module carries its product, PCB revision, serial number and production date in a write-once record. MuraLink shows the Manufacturer, the Serial number, the Board with its revision and the Firmware on Device > Status, and the board on the device line of the Overview. Over the control interface, *IDN? reports the serial number as its third field, for example JP150-0001-0005; SYS:BOARD:RECORD? shows the whole record and SYS:BOARD:TYPE? the board the firmware recognised.

docs.title: The safe state
docs.text:
A board without a record the firmware supports (a bare development board, a record of another product, or a revision newer than the firmware knows) starts in a safe state:

  • The DSP and both power stages stay in reset; there is no audio.
  • The status LED shows red with a dim white step every second.
  • MuraLink shows a banner, keeps the identification and the firmware update available and limits its polling to the commands that still answer.
  • Over the control interface only the identification and update commands answer (*IDN?, ping, the SYS:BOARD:* queries, version and diagnostics queries, SYS:BOOTLOADER); every other command answers ERR:BOARD:UNSUPPORTED.

The point of the safe state is that such a module can still be identified and updated to a firmware that supports it.

docs.title: 12 V trigger
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.4since 26.10.12026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

PCB 1.4 has a trigger input for the usual 12 V trigger signal of a preamplifier or source, or for a push button. The firmware offers three modes. On PCB 1.3 the settings are accepted and stored but have no effect.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text: Mode Behaviour OFF (default) The input is ignored. FOLLOW A change to high returns the module to NORMAL; a change to low takes it to the trigger target level. The level found at start counts too: a module started without a trigger powers down about 5 s after start, and switching to FOLLOW applies the current level at once. The encoder and the control interface still override, until the trigger changes again. ONOFF The input is a push button. A press while powered down wakes the module; a press that begins in NORMAL and is held for one second powers it down. The press that wakes never powers down, and the level found at start is not a press.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Values Default Mode OFF, FOLLOW, ONOFF OFF Target level PWRSTAGE_IDLE, PWRSTAGE_OFF, SLEEP, STANDBY SLEEP Priority over automatic decisions on, off on

All three settings are stored and survive a power cycle. With the priority on, in FOLLOW mode, the automatic decisions never contradict the trigger: no silence power-down while the trigger is high, no audio wake while it is low. With it off, automatic power-down and the audio wake work as before, beside the trigger.

A new level counts after 0.1 to 0.2 s; shorter pulses change nothing. Nothing is acted on in the first 5 s after start. A SigmaStudio session on the DSP bus and a pending power-stage retry take precedence over the trigger.

docs.title: In MuraLink
docs.text:
Device > Power Modes, section 12 V Trigger: Trigger input shows the level read at the input, Mode and Power down to set the mode and the target level, and the check box Trigger overrides automatic power-down and audio wake is the priority; Apply trigger settings sends the three to the module. On a board without the input the section is greyed out.

Device > Power Modes: the power level, the automatic power-down and, on PCB 1.4, the 12 V trigger.

docs.title: Over the control interface
docs.text:
Setting Commands Input level SYS:TRIG? answers 1, 0, or N/A on PCB 1.3 Mode SYS:TRIG:MODE?, SYS:TRIG:MODE with OFF, FOLLOW or ONOFF Target level SYS:TRIG:TARGET?, SYS:TRIG:TARGET with the level Priority SYS:TRIG:PRIORITY?, SYS:TRIG:PRIORITY with 0 or 1

The syntax and the answers are in the SYS:TRIG reference.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text: JST PH, 2 pins (12V TRIGGER): pin 1 trigger, pin 2 GND. 3.3 V to 12 V reads as active; the input has a series resistor and a 3.3 V clamp. See Connectors and pinouts.

docs.title: Volume and encoder
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-03Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF datasheetJP150 Datasheet & User Guide, revision 0.6 · 8.8 MB

docs.title: The encoder
docs.text: The optional rotary encoder on the ENCODER connector controls the module without a PC: rotate to change the master volume, press to cycle the active input. Disabled inputs are skipped. In any power-down level, a turn or a press wakes the module; that first action only wakes it and does not also change the volume or the input, which you cannot see while powered down. Holding the button while switching the module on enters the bootloader's update mode (Recovery).

docs.title: Volume
docs.text: The master volume (0 to 99) applies to both power stages; each stage also has its own volume. Volume changes are saved automatically a few seconds after the last change and restored at the next power-up. With the Wi-Fi input, the module's volume and the Wi-Fi module's volume are synchronised only during active playback, and the module's volume wins when a source connects.

docs.title: Mute, clip and faults
docs.text: Each power stage can be muted by hardware and reports clipping and faults; the worst fault since the last clear is kept as the latched fault until it is cleared. On PCB 1.4 clipping and faults are also shown by the yellow and red LEDs next to the power stages (Indicators and LEDs).

docs.title: In MuraLink
docs.text:
• Everyday use: the Volume slider and Mute on the Overview; Mute silences the output.
  • Per stage: Power stage > Controls has the Master volume, the Stage volume of AMP0 and AMP1 (together with Link AMP0 / AMP1, or one at a time) and the step of the ± buttons.
  • Status and faults: Power stage > Status shows, per stage, Hardware mute (applies at once), Clipping, the Error pin, the decoded Fault and the Latched fault with its Clear button, and offers Hold in reset and Reset amplifier for a stage that needs a reset to recover.
Power stage > Controls: the master volume and the stage volumes. Power stage > Status: hardware mute, clipping and faults per stage.

docs.title: Over the control interface
docs.text:
Task Commands Master volume AMP:VOL?, AMP:VOL with 0 to 99 Volume of one stage AMP0:VOL?, AMP0:VOL; AMP1:VOL?, AMP1:VOL Hardware mute of a stage AMP0:HWMUTE?, AMP0:HWMUTE with 0 or 1; the same for AMP1 Clipping within the last 500 ms AMP0:CLIP?, AMP1:CLIP? Fault state AMP0:FAULT? (live), AMP0:FAULT:LATCHED? (the worst since the last clear), AMP0:ERROR? (the FAULT pin); the same for AMP1 Clear or recover AMP0:FAULT:CLEAR, AMP0:FAULT:RECOVER (a reset pulse); AMP0:RESET holds the stage in reset; the same for AMP1

The answers and the fault names are in the AMP reference.

docs.title: Release 26.10.1
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Released 2026-10-18. Changes since release 26.8.0; the intermediate versions 26.9.0 and 26.10.0 were not published. The first release with the improved bootloader and firmware updates from MuraLink, PCB 1.4 support, Bluetooth TWS with a remembered partner, safer settings, a faster start-up and MURA LABS' own USB identity.

Before you update

Modules with PCB revision 1.4 are delivered with firmware 26.10.1. A module with PCB revision 1.3 that runs 26.8.0 cannot install this release over USB by itself: contact support, the first update is arranged individually. Never use the old FirmwareUpdater or DIP switch 3 on a module that runs 26.10.1 or later.

docs.title: Improved bootloader and firmware updates from MuraLink
docs.text:
The module now runs an improved bootloader that installs the update bundles MuraLink provides. The bootloader checks each package before it changes anything, installs the firmware and verifies it at every start-up. An update that is interrupted, by a pulled cable or a power loss, leaves the module waiting in update mode: repeat the update and nothing is lost.

  • Updating with MuraLink. Open the update bundle (JPx_Update_26.10.1.zip) on MuraLink's firmware update page. MuraLink checks the bundle against the module, restarts the module into update mode, installs the package and reconnects when the module has restarted. The whole update takes about a minute. No driver, no DIP switch and no separate updater are needed. See Update with MuraLink.
  • Indication on the module. In update mode the status LED blinks amber; during the transfer the level meter fills blue; steady green means installed and restarting; blinking red means the update failed and can be repeated. See LED indication.
  • Recovery without a PC command. Holding the encoder button while switching the module on enters update mode. A module without valid firmware, or one whose firmware failed to start three times in a row, waits in update mode by itself. A module sent into update mode by command returns to its firmware after 5 minutes if no update follows.
  • Rollback protection. A package older than the module's security floor is refused. Production modules are sealed (read-out protection level 2): their debug port and the ST ROM bootloader are closed, so the update bundle is the only way to change the firmware.

docs.title: PCB revision 1.4 supported, one firmware for both revisions
docs.text:
26.10.1 runs on PCB revision 1.3 and 1.4 and recognises the board from its factory record. What revision 1.4 adds, as far as the firmware is concerned:

  • 12 V trigger input. A 3.3 V to 12 V signal on the new trigger connector, with the modes OFF, FOLLOW and ONOFF, a target level and a priority over the automatic power decisions. See 12 V trigger.
  • Accurate supply monitoring. Voltage and current come from a dedicated power monitor, and a power reading (SYS:MEAS:POW?) joins them. On PCB 1.3 the readings stay as before.
  • USB-C power sensing (SYS:POWER:USBC?). The firmware reports whether a USB-C power source is present.
  • DSP boot memory written from the PC. The DSP program memory of PCB 1.4 is written over the module's USB connection, by MuraLink or as part of a firmware update, so a USBi programmer is no longer required to install the default DSP program.
  • No configuration DIP switch. Its three functions moved: the DSP self-boot setting is a stored firmware setting (DSP:SELFBOOT), the master clock is selected by the firmware, and the MCU boot pin is a factory-only solder jumper. The hardware differences, connector pinouts included, are on Connectors and pinouts.

docs.title: Board identity from the factory record
docs.text: Every provisioned module carries its product, PCB revision, serial number and production date in a write-once record. *IDN? now reports that serial number (for example JP150-0001-0005), and MuraLink shows the board type next to it. A module without a supported record, for example a bare development board, starts in a safe state: outputs muted, status LED red with a dim white step every second, and only the identification and update commands available, so that it can still be updated.

docs.title: Bluetooth TWS remembers its partner
docs.text: A TWS pair now survives power cycles. The two modules reconnect automatically when they are switched on, in any order, and the roles are called Primary (the module the phone connects to) and Secondary instead of master and slave. The stored role became the Fallback Role: it is used only when no partner is remembered. MuraLink's Bluetooth section gained a TWS page with the pairing status, the remembered devices and the actions Start New Pairing, Disconnect, Reconnect and Forget Peer. The complete procedure is in TWS: pairing two units. The status LED patterns are unchanged: green accent for the Primary, purple-red for the Secondary.

docs.title: Settings: safer autosave and a settings reset
docs.text: Settings are saved automatically as before, and a change made right before a restart or a firmware update is now written first instead of being lost. A new command, SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS (MuraLink: Reset settings), returns the user settings to their defaults and restarts the module: the volumes, the input enable mask, the automatic power-down, the DSP self-boot setting and the trigger settings. The selected input, the TWS Fallback Role, the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi pairings and the DSP program are kept.

docs.title: Faster, cleaner start-up
docs.text: The module no longer waits up to six seconds for the DSP before anything else runs: the LEDs, the encoder and the control interface respond immediately after power-on, and the level meter no longer shows random colours meanwhile. Audio starts as soon as the DSP has loaded its program, about 50 ms after power-on on PCB 1.4 and 200 to 250 ms on PCB 1.3. Waking from sleep or standby restarts the DSP the same way, so audio returns within about a second.

docs.title: Task watchdog
docs.text: A watchdog now supervises every firmware task. A module that stops responding restarts itself instead of staying silent, and the cause is visible afterwards (SYS:RESET:CAUSE? answers IWDG).

docs.title: New USB identity
docs.text: The module identifies itself with MURA LABS' own USB IDs: 16D0:15B8 for the application (USB Audio and the virtual COM port) and 16D0:15B7 for update mode; 26.8.0 used 0483:5741. Windows installs no driver for either. After the change the PC sees a new device, and the COM port number can change.

docs.title: Diagnostics for support
docs.text: New read-only queries report the cause of the last reset, how the bootloader started the firmware, the installed package (release, special build or development, with its security counter), the protection state of the module, the DSP boot result and core state, and the health of the operating system. See Changes by release.

docs.title: Fixed issues
docs.text:
• KI-07 A setting changed right before a restart or an update could be lost
  • KI-06 Wrong input after waking from sleep or standby
  • KI-03 Supply current reading is indicative only
  • KI-02 Seconds of random level-meter colours at power-up
  • KI-01 TWS pairing sometimes unstable confirmation pending
  • Wrong input after waking from sleep or standby (PCB 1.4). The DSP of PCB 1.4 reloads its program on every wake, and the module re-sent the selected input before the program was ready, so the DSP played its default source, the test tone, while the status LED showed the right input. The input is now sent once the DSP program is running.
  • Seconds of random level-meter colours at power-up. Before the firmware responded to anything, the level meter showed whatever its LEDs latched at power-on, for up to six seconds, because the start-up waited for the DSP. The wait is gone. This also applied to PCB 1.3.
  • A setting changed right before a restart or an update could be lost. Settings are written a few seconds after a change. A restart, the entry into update mode or a reset command that came within that time lost the change. Pending changes are now written first.
  • Supply current reading was indicative only. Fixed on PCB 1.4 by the new power monitor. The PCB 1.3 reading is unchanged and stays indicative.
  • TWS pairing was sometimes unstable. The Bluetooth firmware no longer clears the pairing at every start and re-pairs from scratch, which is what made a pair fail to form or misbehave. The modules keep their pairing and reconnect to it.

docs.title: Audio processing (DSP)
docs.text:
• Default DSP program delivered with the firmware. The basic pass-through design of 26.8.0 is unchanged and is now part of the firmware update bundle for PCB 1.4, exported for the module's SPI boot memory with a boot read clock of 5 MHz. During a firmware update MuraLink asks whether to write it and never writes it unasked, so an own DSP design stays in place unless you choose otherwise. The same program is written at the factory.
  • Writing your own design on PCB 1.4. A SigmaStudio project is downloaded to the running DSP through the USBi as before. To write it into the boot memory of PCB 1.4, either let MuraLink write the SigmaStudio self-boot export, or write it from SigmaStudio through the DSP with the new memory settings. See Writing the boot memory.
  • Dedicated DSP bus on PCB 1.4. On PCB 1.4 the DSP has its own control bus, separate from the power stages and the settings memory. The programmer detection of 26.8.0 applies to that bus.

docs.title: Updating to 26.10.1
docs.text:
• PCB revision 1.4. Modules are delivered with firmware 26.10.1 and the default DSP program. Later releases are installed with MuraLink from their update bundle.
  • PCB revision 1.3. A PCB 1.3 module on 26.8.0 cannot install 26.10.1 or any later release over USB by itself. The first update is arranged with support; afterwards the module updates with MuraLink like a PCB 1.4 module.
  • MuraLink. Use MuraLink 26.10.1, delivered with this release as MuraLink_26.10.1.zip. The executable now brings its .NET runtime along, so nothing has to be installed first (Install). Older versions connect, but they do not know the update bundle, the DSP boot memory or the new TWS controls.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text: The living list is on Known issues. Open at the time of this release: the control bus guard after a SigmaStudio session (PCB 1.4), the module not knowing which DSP program it runs, the front LEDs on some PCB 1.4 modules, the lone TWS unit not reconnecting the phone, the external master clock, and the carried-over USB and power-down behaviours.

docs.title: Control interface
docs.text: 52 commands added, 4 removed (DSP:AUTOLOAD, DSP:AUTOLOAD?, BT:BOOTROLE, BT:BOOTROLE?), 10 with changed behaviour. The list is on Changes by release; what a host must handle is on Integration notes.

docs.title: Stored settings
docs.text: The settings-memory layout changed from version 3 to version 6. On the first start of 26.10.1 the stored settings are rebuilt once (SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE? answers NODATA on that start, OK from the next one): the input enable mask returns to all inputs enabled, the automatic power-down to its defaults (off, 1800 s, PWRSTAGE_OFF, threshold 5), the DSP self boot to on and the 12 V trigger to OFF / SLEEP / priority 1. Master volume, channel volumes, the selected input and the TWS fallback role are kept.

docs.title: Release 26.6.2
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.2PCB 1.32026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Released 2026-06-21 for PCB revisions 1.2 and 1.3: the first release with the yy.mm.r version scheme, and the oldest release this site documents. Its 108 commands are the baseline of the command reference; a command marked "since 26.6.2" may be older. The release had no What's New document; this summary comes from the firmware history.

docs.title: What the release brought
docs.text:
• Control over USB. The module enumerates as one composite USB device: USB audio and a virtual COM port that carries the same control command set as the UART. Before, the control interface was available over UART only.
  • Settings memory. The driver of the on-board settings EEPROM of PCB 1.3, whose presence also told the firmware the PCB revision; PCB 1.2 has no settings memory. The automatic saving of settings came with 26.7.0.
  • True Wireless Stereo. The first working TWS between two modules, with the status LED patterns that show the pairing and the role.
  • Level meter. The six-LED level meter fed by the DSP program.

docs.title: Known issues at the time

docs.title: Release 26.7.0
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.32026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Released 2026-07-03 for PCB revision 1.3. Changes since release 26.6.2, reconstructed after the fact from the datasheet revision 0.4 that was published with it; the release had no What's New document of its own.

docs.title: Settings saved automatically
docs.text: The master volume and the selected input are written to the settings memory a few seconds after a change and restored at the next power-up, by a task of its own so that the audio path is never disturbed. A production command stores the board's revision and serial number, which the firmware reports on request (Settings and memory).

docs.title: Power-stage control and monitoring
docs.text: Each TAS3251 power stage gained hardware mute and reset over the control interface, decoded fault reporting (live state, worst fault since the last clear, a clear and a recovery command) and clock and PLL diagnostics. The power-stage temperature (TMP112) and the supply current are measured and reported, with minima and maxima (Volume and encoder, command reference).

docs.title: DSP parameters through the IPAT
docs.text: Input selection goes through the DSP program's indirect parameter access table instead of fixed addresses, a host can write any exposed parameter the same way (DSP:IPAT:SETBLOCK), and the level meter's RMS value is readable (DSP:LVLMETER:RMS?). An own DSP design keeps the starter project's table entries (IPAT and parameters).

docs.title: S/PDIF DC offset removed
docs.text: A high-pass filter in the DSP path removes the DC offset of the S/PDIF input.

docs.title: Fixed issues
docs.text:
No known issue of the previous releases is closed by this release.

  • A stalled I2S transmit DMA is detected and recovered instead of leaving the output silent.
  • The control UART and the Wi-Fi module's UART recover by themselves after a UART error.
  • The Bluetooth module's serial framing was rewritten; it resynchronises after an error and is safe across buffer wrap, which fixes playback recovery after a module restart.
  • The volume synchronisation with the Wi-Fi module compared in the wrong direction and padded the volume incorrectly.
  • The Wi-Fi module reload is pulsed from task context, and holding the encoder button fires once per press.
  • DSP:SETBLOCK, BT:DEVNAME and the Wi-Fi mode queries validate their parameters.

docs.text: 20 commands added, 2 removed (AMP0:RST and AMP1:RST, replaced by the pin-level AMP0:RESET and AMP1:RESET and the fault commands). The list is on Changes by release.

docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.32026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Released 2026-08-25 for PCB revision 1.3. Changes since release 26.7.0. Published at the time as the PDF "What's New WN-2.0"; this page is its content.

docs.title: Automatic power-down with wake-on-audio
docs.text:
The amplifier can watch for silence and drop into a lower power state after a configurable period, returning to normal when audio comes back. The feature is disabled by default.

  • Target level: four levels, each switching off progressively more. Delay: 10 s to 18 h, default 30 min. Sensitivity: by default only true digital silence counts as silent; raise it if your source leaves a residual signal and the amplifier never powers down.
  • Wakes on an encoder turn or press, audio returning, a SigmaStudio programmer, or any reset. The click that wakes the unit only wakes it.
  • Silence is measured at the source, before the volume control. A muted power stage still being fed audio will not power down; paused audio does count as silence.
  • How deep it goes depends on the selected input: USB and Bluetooth reach standby, Wi-Fi reaches sleep, S/PDIF and I2S reach power stage off, the sine generator never powers down. See Automatic power-down.

docs.title: Sleep now keeps the Wi-Fi module powered
docs.text: Sleep previously switched off the Wi-Fi module, making it electrically identical to standby and dropping the amplifier off the network. Sleep now keeps it powered, so the unit stays reachable and wakes when you play to it; standby is the only level that removes it. See Power levels.

docs.title: Switch individual inputs on and off
docs.text: Each of the six inputs can be enabled or disabled individually. A disabled input is skipped when cycling with the rotary encoder and refused over the control interface. At least one input always stays enabled; switching off the active input moves to the next enabled one. Remembered across power cycles.

docs.title: Safe coexistence with a SigmaStudio programmer
docs.text: The amplifier detects a programmer on the shared control bus within milliseconds and stands down until it finishes, so downloads and live tuning no longer need the amplifier idle or specially prepared. The level meter freezes meanwhile, automatic power-down is suspended, and a stuck bus is reported separately. See Programmer coexistence.

docs.title: Clearer indication in power-down modes
docs.text: In any power-down mode the power LED dims to a short flash every two seconds, the status LED switches off and restores on waking, and the level meter clears.

docs.title: Fixed issues
docs.text:
• Volume jump when selecting the Wi-Fi input. The module reported its factory default while idle or in configuration mode. Volume now synchronises only during active playback, and the amplifier's volume wins when a source connects.
  • USB audio stopped working after the computer went idle. After a host suspend the amplifier never responded to USB again until a power cycle. It now resumes normally after any suspend.
  • Amplifier could stop responding if a power stage failed to start. Attempts are now time-limited and retried in the background, and a fault in one power stage no longer prevents the other from working.
  • Unconfigured power stage could run loud. A power stage that cannot be configured is kept muted rather than unmuted; the amplifier retries in the background.
  • Spurious hardware clipping fault in PBTL mode. The power stage is held muted and in reset from the first instruction after reset, and the supply rail comes up once and stays up.
  • Wrong input after waking from sleep. The selection is re-applied automatically while the outputs are still muted.

docs.title: Audio processing (DSP)
docs.text: The standard pass-through design was streamlined and restructured, with no audible change: input and output blocks handle input selection, sample-rate conversion, metering and routing, and the main schematic has a dedicated area for your own processing. Removing eight redundant software mute stages freed about 11 % of DSP program memory.

docs.title: Control interface
docs.text: Thirteen commands added (the input enable mask, the automatic power-down policy, the I2C bus guard), two changed (SYS:INPUT now answers; SYS:POWER:AUTO became functional). The stored settings layout changed, so existing values were discarded once on update. See Changes by release and Integration notes.

docs.title: Known issues at the time
docs.text: TWS pairing sometimes unstable; supply current measurement indicative only; MCLK always internal; brief digital noise when USB audio resumes after a long silence; a USB source streaming silence keeps the amplifier awake; some sources prevent automatic power-down; standby saves less power than the name suggests; on-board indicators can flicker; level metering unavailable in sleep and standby. Their current state is on Known issues.

One living list. Each entry names the boards it affects, the workaround where there is one, and the release that fixed it. An issue is never removed: when a release fixes it, it moves to the fixed list below and appears in that release's notes.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• KI-11Front LEDs show white or random colours on some PCB 1.4 modules open PCB 1.4

    On part of the first PCB 1.4 production batch the power LED, status LED and level meter show white or random colours after power-on instead of their patterns. Audio and the control interface are not affected. The LED type used on PCB 1.4 is more sensitive to the drive timing than the earlier type; a firmware fix is in preparation.

    reported 2026-10-31 · since firmware 26.10.1

  • KI-10Control bus guard can stay active after a SigmaStudio session open PCB 1.4

    After a SigmaStudio download through the USBi, the module can keep treating the DSP bus as busy until it is reset, even with the USBi unplugged. DSP queries then answer ERROR, and an input or power-mode change does not reach the DSP although the status LED follows it.

    Workaround. Reset or power-cycle the module after using the USBi.

    reported 2026-10-12 · since firmware 26.10.1

  • KI-09The module does not know which DSP program it runs open

    The firmware keeps no record of the program written to the DSP boot memory, so MuraLink cannot show it, and its update question cannot tell an own program from the default one.

    reported 2026-10-12 · since firmware 26.10.1

  • KI-08A lone TWS unit does not reconnect the phone by itself open

    When a paired unit is switched on without its partner, it plays on its own, but the connection to the phone is not restored automatically.

    Workaround. Connect from the phone's Bluetooth settings; the partner joins when it is switched on.

    reported 2026-09-15 · since firmware 26.9.0

  • KI-05External master clock is not supported open

    The module always runs from its internal master clock. On PCB 1.3 the DIP switch position has no effect; on PCB 1.4 the firmware keeps the internal clock selected.

    reported 2026-08-25 · since firmware 26.6.2

  • KI-04Brief digital noise when USB audio resumes after a long silence open

    After a longer silence on the USB input, a short burst of digital noise can be audible when the stream resumes. It normally clears by itself within a few seconds.

    reported 2026-08-25 · since firmware 26.6.2

docs.title: Fixed in the current release, confirmation pending
docs.text:
• KI-01TWS pairing sometimes unstable fixed in 26.10.1, confirmation pending

    Pairing two units could fail, and an established pair could misbehave, because the pairing was rebuilt at every start. The pairing is now remembered and reconnected. Bench confirmation on two TWS-capable units is pending.

    Workaround. Reset the Secondary, or both units, for that power cycle.

    reported 2026-08-25 · since firmware 26.6.2

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• KI-07A setting changed right before a restart or an update could be lost fixed in 26.10.1

    Settings are written a few seconds after a change. A restart, the entry into update mode or a reset command that came within that time lost the change. Pending changes are now written first.

    reported 2026-10-12 · since firmware 26.7.0

  • KI-06Wrong input after waking from sleep or standby fixed in 26.10.1 PCB 1.4

    The DSP of PCB 1.4 reloads its program on every wake, and the module re-sent the selected input before the program was ready, so the DSP played its default source, the test tone. The input is now sent once the DSP program is running.

    reported 2026-10-09 · since firmware 26.10.0

  • KI-03Supply current reading is indicative only fixed in 26.10.1

    Fixed on PCB 1.4, which measures with a dedicated power monitor. The PCB 1.3 reading is unchanged and stays indicative; use an external meter where the figure matters.

    reported 2026-08-25 · since firmware 26.7.0

  • KI-02Seconds of random level-meter colours at power-up fixed in 26.10.1

    Before the firmware responded to anything, the level meter showed whatever its LEDs latched at power-on, for up to six seconds, because the start-up waited for the DSP. The wait is gone.

    reported 2026-10-09 · since firmware 26.6.2

Behaviour changes

  1. SYS:BOOTLOADER answers SYS:BOOTLOADER:OK after at most 1 s (pending settings are written first) and restarts the module into the bootloader's update mode: the serial port disappears and a DFU device 16D0:15B7 appears. The ST ROM bootloader is no longer used. Without an update the module returns to its firmware after 5 minutes.
  2. *RST still answers Resetting device... first, then writes pending settings (at most 1 s) and resets at least 100 ms after the answer, so the answer now also arrives over USB.
  3. *IDN? reports the serial number of the factory record as its third field, N/A without a record. On a provisioned module the setter SYS:BOARD:ID answers SYS:BOARD:ID:LOCKED and writes nothing.
  4. On a module without a supported factory record every command outside the reduced set answers ERR:BOARD:UNSUPPORTED, one line without a prefix. The reduced set is marked with a dagger in the reference.
  5. New prefixes of longer commands: BT:TWS:PAIR (:START, :STATUS?), BT:TWS:SCAN? (:COUNT?, :ITEM?, :DIAG?), SYS:BOOTLOADER (:INFO?), SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE? (:PENDING?) and SYS:TRIG? (:MODE?, :TARGET?, :PRIORITY?). A response matcher that works by prefix must exclude the longer forms.
  6. SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO? and SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING? are extensible: later firmware may append fields. Hosts read the fields they know and ignore further ones.
  7. BT:TWS:UNPAIR answers BT:TWS:UNPAIR:OK or :ERR:MODULE; it was silent. BT:TWS:PAIR still blocks the control interface for up to 15 s: use BT:TWS:PAIR:START and poll BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS?.
  8. BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE? answers Standalone, Primary or Secondary; the removed BT:BOOTROLE? answered Master and Slave. The numeric values of the setter are unchanged.
  9. SYS:MEAS:VOLT? and SYS:MEAS:CURR? keep their format. On PCB 1.4 they draw no answer when the power monitor cannot be read.
  10. DSP:PC:ADVANCING? keeps its name and answer, but now reports 1 while the DSP core runs or sleeps between samples, from one status register. It used to sample the program counter, which also moves while no program runs.
  11. The virtual COM port enumerates under USB 16D0:15B8 (was 0483:5741), update mode under 16D0:15B7. Software that finds the module by VID and PID must add the new identifiers.
  12. The settings-memory layout changed (version 3 to 6). On the first start of 26.10.1 the stored settings are rebuilt once: SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE? answers NODATA on that start, and the input enable mask, the automatic power-down and the new settings return to their defaults; volumes, the selected input and the TWS fallback role are kept.
  13. BT:AT is unfiltered: it will send AT+RESTORE (factory reset of the Bluetooth module) or AT+BAUD (breaks the link). A development aid, not a product feature.

Behaviour of firmware 26.10.1 that host software must handle. The protocol page has the general rules; Changes by release lists, for every release, the commands added and removed and the behaviour changes, generated from the firmware's command tables.

docs.title: Matching answers
docs.text:
Answers carry the command as their prefix (AMP:VOL:32), and several commands are prefixes of longer ones: SYS:INPUT of SYS:INPUT:ENABLE, SYS:TRIG? of SYS:TRIG:MODE?, BT:TWS:PAIR of BT:TWS:PAIR:START, SYS:BOOTLOADER of SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO?, SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE? of SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING?, BT:TWS:SCAN? of BT:TWS:SCAN:COUNT?. A matcher that pairs answers with requests by prefix must match the whole prefix up to the value, and must know that some setters answer with the prefix of their query (SYS:INPUT:OK). Answers marked extensible in the reference (SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO?, SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING?) may grow by fields at the end: read the fields you know and ignore the rest.

A command the firmware does not know draws no answer at all. On a module whose board the firmware does not support, every command outside the reduced set answers the line ERR:BOARD:UNSUPPORTED without a prefix; the reduced set is marked in the command reference.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
The control interface runs the commands in order, and a few of them hold it for a while:

Command Holds the interface for SYS:POWER:MODE NORMAL from PWRSTAGE_OFF, SLEEP or STANDBY about 350 ms plus the power-stage initialisation AMPx:FAULT:RECOVER the 5 ms reset pulse BT:TWS:PAIR up to 15 s (use BT:TWS:PAIR:START and poll BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS?) BT:TWS:PAIR:START about 0.7 s BT:TWS:PEERLIST?, BT:AT the module's settle time, 0.5 s for BT:AT SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS up to about 2.2 s, then the module restarts 500 ms after the answer SYS:NVM:FLASH:SAVE, SYS:NVM:FLASH:ERASE 1 to 2 s when a flash sector is erased DSP:FLASH:ERASE, DSP:FLASH:CRC? up to 8 s per 64 KB erased; about 16 s per MB checked *RST, SYS:BOOTLOADER the answer comes first; the restart follows within about 1 s

A host allows for these in its timeouts rather than treating them as a lost connection.

docs.title: Stored settings
docs.text:
The settings-memory layout changed from version 3 to version 6 in 26.10.1. On the first start of 26.10.1 the stored settings are rebuilt once (SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE? answers NODATA on that start, OK from the next one): the input enable mask returns to all inputs enabled, the automatic power-down to its defaults (off, 1800 s, PWRSTAGE_OFF, threshold 5), the DSP self boot to on and the 12 V trigger to OFF / SLEEP / priority 1. Master volume, channel volumes, the selected input and the TWS fallback role are kept.

The autosave writes a setting once it has stayed unchanged for its debounce: 0.1 s for the self boot and the trigger settings, 1 s for the input enable flags and the fallback role, 2 s for the input, 3 s for the volumes, 5 s for the automatic power-down settings. SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING? answers 1 while a write is outstanding; *RST and SYS:BOOTLOADER write pending settings first.

SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS returns the user settings to their defaults and restarts the module: the volumes, the input enable mask, the automatic power-down settings, the DSP self boot and the three trigger settings. The selected input, the TWS fallback role, the board identity, the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi pairings and the DSP program are kept. The answer can take about 2 s; the module restarts 500 ms after it.

docs.title: Finding the module
docs.text: The firmware's virtual COM port enumerates under USB 16D0:15B8 (firmware before 26.10.1: 0483:5741) and the bootloader's update mode under 16D0:15B7. UART1 runs at 115200 8N1 and serves the same commands. *IDN? identifies a module; SYS:BOARD:TYPE? tells whether the board is supported.

docs.text: Transport Settings User UART (UART1) 115200 bit/s, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, 3.3 V logic (RX 5 V tolerant). Pinout: Connectors. USB virtual COM port Part of the module's composite USB device (16D0:15B8 from firmware 26.10.1, 0483:5741 before). No driver on Windows 10 and 11. Any baud rate.

docs.title: Command format
docs.text:
Commands are ASCII strings. Queries end with ?. Set commands omit the ? and carry their argument after a space; several arguments are separated by commas. Terminate every command with CRLF and parse responses as single-line ASCII strings, also CRLF-terminated.

Most query responses repeat the command prefix, followed by a colon and the value: AMP:VOL? answers AMP:VOL:32. Action and set commands answer a status string (<CMD>:OK, or <CMD>:ERR:<REASON> when refused) or execute without a reply, as the reference notes per command.

SYS:INPUT?              →  SYS:INPUT:BT
SYS:INPUT WIFI          →  SYS:INPUT:OK
AMP:VOL 32              →  (no reply)
SYS:POWER:AUTO:DELAY?   →  SYS:POWER:AUTO:DELAY:1800
SYS:TRIG:MODE FOLLOW    →  (no reply)

A set command that is refused answers with an error string rather than falling silent, for example SYS:INPUT:ERR:DISABLED. Treat any value field that begins with ERR as a rejected command, and do not assume the setting changed.

docs.title: Rules for a robust host
docs.text:
• Match responses on the whole prefix. Several commands are prefixes of longer ones (SYS:INPUT and SYS:INPUT:ENABLE, BT:TWS:PAIR and BT:TWS:PAIR:START, SYS:BOOTLOADER and SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO?).
  • Expect unrequested changes. The module changes its power level on its own (automatic power-down, wake sources, the 12 V trigger), so an unrequested change is normal.
  • Allow time after a power level change. Returning from a level that removed power from the power stages takes several hundred milliseconds without a reply.
  • Read extensible answers by position. SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO? and SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING? may gain fields at the end; read the fields you know.
  • Treat ERR:BOARD:UNSUPPORTED as "exists but unavailable". A module in the safe state answers it to every command outside its reduced set (Start-up and the safe state).
  • A missing reply is not always an error. SYS:MEAS:VOLT? and SYS:MEAS:CURR? draw no answer on PCB 1.4 when the supply monitor cannot be read; treat it as a sensor failure.
  • Do not use the blocking pairing command. BT:TWS:PAIR holds the control interface for up to 15 s; use BT:TWS:PAIR:START and poll BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS?.

docs.title: Reading the tables
docs.text:
• Parameter uses <name> for a value to fill in, 0..99 for a range and 0, 1 for the choices; a dash means the command takes none. Several parameters are separated by commas, as on the wire.
  • Answer is the line the module sends; no answer marks a setter that sends nothing. An invalid parameter is an SCPI error: no answer at all, which a host can tell from a slow module only by its timeout while ping still answers.
  • Since is the release the command appeared in. 26.6.2 is the oldest release documented here, so a command marked 26.6.2 may be older.
  • Boards are the PCB revisions the command applies to. Where a command answers N/A on one revision, the column says so.
  • † marks the 24 commands that are also served in the safe state, the reduced set of a module whose board the firmware does not support (SYS:BOARD:TYPE?); every other command then answers ERR:BOARD:UNSUPPORTED.
  • Stored settings are written to the settings memory by the autosave; SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING? shows a pending write and SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS resets the user settings.

docs.title: AMP:VOL
docs.text:
Commands: AMP:VOL?, AMP:VOL

The master volume applies to both channels. A value above 99 is an SCPI error and changes nothing. The volume is a stored setting (autosave after 3 s without a change).

AMP:VOL?    ->  AMP:VOL:32
AMP:VOL 40

docs.title: AMP0:VOL, AMP1:VOL
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:VOL?, AMP0:VOL, AMP1:VOL?, AMP1:VOL

The channel volumes, 0 to 99 each, on top of the master volume. Stored settings, like the master volume. AMP0 and AMP1 follow the same rules throughout this page.

docs.title: AMP0:HWMUTE, AMP1:HWMUTE
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:HWMUTE?, AMP0:HWMUTE, AMP1:HWMUTE?, AMP1:HWMUTE

Drives the MUTE pin of the power stage (1 = muted). The query reads back the last commanded level, not a register. A value above 1 is an SCPI error.

docs.title: AMP0:RESET, AMP1:RESET
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:RESET?, AMP0:RESET, AMP1:RESET?, AMP1:RESET

Drives the RESET pin of the power stage (1 = held in reset); the query reads back the last commanded level. While the reset is asserted, and for about 250 ms after it is released, AMPx:ERROR? reads 0 and AMPx:FAULT? reports MASKED, because the FAULT pin is not meaningful then. Releasing the reset also clears the latched fault. A value above 1 is an SCPI error.

docs.title: AMP0:CLIP?, AMP1:CLIP?
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:CLIP?, AMP1:CLIP?

1 when a clip pulse of the power stage was sampled within the last 500 ms. The firmware samples the CLIP_OTW pin at 10 kHz and holds the indication for 500 ms, so a host polling once a second still sees short clips.

docs.title: AMP0:ERROR?, AMP1:ERROR?
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:ERROR?, AMP1:ERROR?

The raw level of the FAULT pin, 1 = fault asserted. 0 while the power stage is in reset and during the 250 ms settling window after it. For the decoded cause use AMPx:FAULT?.

docs.title: AMP0:FAULT?, AMP1:FAULT?
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:FAULT?, AMP1:FAULT?

The fault state decoded from the FAULT and CLIP_OTW pins of the TAS3251. A steady over-temperature warning is told apart from clip pulses by a 30 ms continuous-low detector on CLIP_OTW.

Power-stage fault states

Value Meaning NONE No fault OTW Over-temperature warning only, no shutdown OLP_UVP FAULT asserted below the warning temperature, overload or undervoltage OTE FAULT asserted with a steady over-temperature warning, thermal shutdown MASKED The power stage is in reset or in the 250 ms settling window after it; the FAULT pin is not meaningful then 
AMP0:FAULT?  ->  AMP0:FAULT:NONE
AMP1:FAULT?  ->  AMP1:FAULT:OTW

docs.title: AMP0:FAULT:LATCHED?, AMP1:FAULT:LATCHED?
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:FAULT:LATCHED?, AMP1:FAULT:LATCHED?

The most severe fault seen since the last clear, kept by the 10 kHz sampler, so a fault that came and went between two polls is still reported. Only asserted faults are latched: the answer is NONE, OLP_UVP or OTE, never OTW or MASKED. Cleared by AMPx:FAULT:CLEAR and when a reset of the power stage is released.

docs.title: AMP0:FAULT:CLEAR, AMP1:FAULT:CLEAR
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:FAULT:CLEAR, AMP1:FAULT:CLEAR

Clears the state read by AMPx:FAULT:LATCHED?. The hardware is not touched: a fault that is still present latches again at the next sample.

docs.title: AMP0:FAULT:RECOVER, AMP1:FAULT:RECOVER
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:FAULT:RECOVER, AMP1:FAULT:RECOVER

The recovery the TAS3251 data sheet prescribes for a latched fault: the reset is asserted for 5 ms and released. The channel drops out for the pulse and the settling window after it. The control interface waits for the pulse.

docs.title: AMP0:CLOCK?, AMP1:CLOCK?
docs.text:
Commands: AMP0:CLOCK?, AMP1:CLOCK?

A snapshot of the TAS3251 clock registers, read over I2C on request. PLL 1 = locked; CDST the clock-detector status bits; CLKERR the clock-error flags; FS the detected sample-rate code; RATIO the detected MCLK/LRCLK ratio code (TAS3251 data sheet, registers 0x5B, 0x5E and 0x5F). Reading the error register clears its latched flags, so this query consumes them. A read failure is an SCPI error.

AMP0:CLOCK?  ->  AMP0:CLOCK:PLL:1,CDST:0x00,CLKERR:0x00,FS:0x6,RATIO:0x8

docs.title: BT:TWS:ENABLED
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:ENABLED?, BT:TWS:ENABLED

The module stores the capability itself, so it survives power cycles. Switching it off tears down a peer link; the peer-link state then reads Standby and the remembered peer is kept. A value above 1 is an SCPI error. The pairing commands switch the capability on when needed.

BT:TWS:ENABLED?  ->  BT:TWS:ENABLED:1
BT:TWS:ENABLED 1

docs.title: BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE?, BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE

Consulted at start only when no peer is remembered; a remembered peer is reconnected instead. Changing it does not change the current session: BT:TWS:REBOOT applies a role now, and BT:TWS:REPAIR sets and applies one in one step. An out-of-range value is an SCPI error. A stored setting (autosave after 1 s). Replaces BT:BOOTROLE, whose query answered Master and Slave.

Default: 1.

Fallback roles

Value Meaning 0 Standalone, no TWS; the module behaves as a single Bluetooth speaker 1 Primary; searches for a peer when none is remembered at start 2 Secondary; waits to be found by a Primary 
BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE?  ->  BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE:Primary
BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE 1

docs.title: BT:TWS:STATE?
docs.text:
A mirror refreshed about every 2 s while the capability is on.

Peer-link states

Value Meaning Unsupported The module does not report a peer link Standby No peer link; also the reading while the TWS capability is off Connecting A peer link is being set up Connected The peer link is up Streaming Audio flows over the peer link 
BT:TWS:STATE?  ->  BT:TWS:STATE:Connected

docs.title: BT:TWS:ROLE?
docs.text:
Unknown until the module has reported its peer record once, and after the pairing was deleted. Distinct from BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE?, the stored intent for the next start.

Live roles

Value Meaning Primary This unit drives the pair Secondary This unit follows the pair Unknown No peer record has been read yet, or the pairing was deleted 
BT:TWS:ROLE?  ->  BT:TWS:ROLE:Primary

docs.title: BT:TWS:PEER?
docs.text:
000000000000 when no peer is remembered.

BT:TWS:PEER?  ->  BT:TWS:PEER:4142DE0BCDAC

docs.title: BT:TWS:BOOTOUTCOME?
docs.text:
Settles once shortly after start, so it belongs on a slow poll. PeerUnreachable is the one worth showing: a peer is remembered but did not answer, so the unit plays alone and keeps doing so until the peer returns or the pair is made again (BT:TWS:REPAIR); without this answer that state looks like never paired.

Start outcomes

BT:TWS:BOOTOUTCOME?  ->  BT:TWS:BOOTOUTCOME:Reconnected

docs.title: BT:TWS:STAT?
docs.text:
All fields numeric: enabled 0/1; state 0 Unsupported, 1 Standby, 2 Connecting, 3 Connected, 4 Streaming; role 0 Secondary, 1 Primary, 2 Unknown; mac the remembered peer or -; fallbackrole 0 to 2; inq 0/1 whether a search runs; pair 0 Idle, 1 Inquiring, 2 OK, 3 NoPeerFound, 4 Error; kept and seen as BT:TWS:SCAN:COUNT?. A read of the firmware's mirror, no traffic to the module: the one query to poll instead of five.

BT:TWS:STAT?  ->  BT:TWS:STAT:1,3,1,4142DE0BCDAC,1,0,2,2,2

docs.title: BT:TWS:PAIR:START, BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS?
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:PAIR:START, BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS?

BT:TWS:PAIR:START drops a phone link, switches the capability on, starts the peer search and returns once the search runs (it holds the control interface for about 0.7 s). ERR:PAIRED: a peer link is already up; ERR:MODULE: the module refused a command, or an attempt is already running. BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS? advances once a second, so the result shows up to a second after the link forms; a final value stays until the next start of a pairing, and BT:TWS:REBOOT resets it to Idle. BT:TWS:INQ 0 aborts a running attempt. This pair of commands replaces BT:TWS:PAIR in host software.

Pairing states

Value Meaning Idle No attempt since start, or reset by BT:TWS:REBOOT Inquiring The search runs OK The peer link reached Connected or Streaming NoPeerFound 15 s passed without a peer; the search was stopped Error The module refused a command of the start sequence 
BT:TWS:PAIR:START    ->  BT:TWS:PAIR:START:OK
BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS?  ->  BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS:Inquiring
BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS?  ->  BT:TWS:PAIR:STATUS:OK

docs.title: BT:TWS:PAIR
docs.text:
The same sequence as BT:TWS:PAIR:START, but the answer waits for the result: the control interface is blocked for up to 15 s, on both the USB and the UART link. Kept for compatibility; use BT:TWS:PAIR:START.

Pairing results

Value Meaning OK The peer link came up within 15 s AlreadyPaired The peer link was already up; nothing was done NoPeerFound 15 s passed without a peer; the search was stopped Error The module refused a command of the sequence 
BT:TWS:PAIR  ->  BT:TWS:PAIR:OK

docs.title: BT:TWS:REPAIR
docs.text:
The software equivalent of the long button press of a commercial TWS speaker, and the command for a remembered peer that has become unreachable. In one action: the new fallback role is stored (ERR:NVM when that write fails, and nothing else is done), the phone links are dropped, the peer memory is wiped, the Bluetooth module is reset with the proper timing, and the role is applied, all without a restart of the amplifier. OK means queued: the sequence runs from the Bluetooth task in the next 4 to 6 s, during which the BT:* mirrors are stale. ERR:BUSY when a request is already pending. MuraLink's Start New Pairing uses it.

BT:TWS:REPAIR 1  ->  BT:TWS:REPAIR:OK

docs.title: BT:TWS:REBOOT
docs.text:
Applies a role immediately instead of at the next start: wipes the pairing, resets and re-powers the module and configures TWS for the role. OK means queued; the sequence takes 4 to 6 s, during which the BT:* mirrors are stale. Does not change BT:TWS:FALLBACKROLE: set both when the role should survive a power cycle, or use BT:TWS:REPAIR. ERR:BUSY when a request is already pending.

BT:TWS:REBOOT 2  ->  BT:TWS:REBOOT:OK

docs.title: BT:TWS:CONN, BT:TWS:DISC
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:CONN, BT:TWS:DISC

BT:TWS:DISC drops the peer link and keeps the pairing, so the pair can come back without pairing again; the module does not reconnect on its own, BT:TWS:CONN does it. The firmware checks before it asks the module, because the module accepts a connect request even without a pairing and then does nothing: ERR:DISABLED with the capability off, ERR:PAIRED with the link already up, ERR:NOPEER without a remembered peer. OK means the request went to the module; the link comes up a few seconds later and shows in BT:TWS:STAT?.

BT:TWS:DISC  ->  BT:TWS:DISC:OK
BT:TWS:CONN  ->  BT:TWS:CONN:OK

docs.title: BT:TWS:BOND:DEL, BT:TWS:UNPAIR
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:BOND:DEL, BT:TWS:UNPAIR

BT:TWS:UNPAIR is BT:TWS:DISC followed by BT:TWS:BOND:DEL. After either, BT:TWS:ROLE? reads Unknown and BT:TWS:STAT? reports - for the peer. The capability stays on so that a later pairing does not need to switch it on. OK confirms that the module accepted the commands, not that the peer noticed.

BT:TWS:UNPAIR  ->  BT:TWS:UNPAIR:OK

docs.title: BT:TWS:INQ
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:INQ?, BT:TWS:INQ

1 starts a search that connects to the first peer found and clears the scan list; 0 stops it, which also aborts a running BT:TWS:PAIR:START. The query is best effort: it tracks the searches the firmware started, and clears when the peer link comes up. A search the module starts on its own is not seen.

BT:TWS:INQ 0  ->  BT:TWS:INQ:OK

docs.title: BT:TWS:REFRESH
docs.text: Asks the module for its capability, link state and peer record at once instead of waiting for the next polling cycle. OK confirms the questions were sent; the answers land within about 1 s and show in BT:TWS:STAT?.

docs.title: BT:TWS:PEERLIST?
docs.text:
The module keeps phone pairings and the TWS peer in one list; istws is 1 for the entry that is the current TWS peer. An empty memory answers 0, so that nothing remembered is stated rather than inferred. The firmware asks the module and waits briefly for the list, so the answer takes a moment. BT:TWS:PEERLIST:ERR:MODULE when the module could not be asked.

BT:TWS:PEERLIST?  ->  BT:TWS:PEERLIST:2;0,4142DE0BCDAC,1,JP150;1,A1B2C3D4E5F6,0,Jan's phone
BT:TWS:PEERLIST?  ->  BT:TWS:PEERLIST:0

docs.title: BT:TWS:SCAN?, BT:TWS:SCAN:COUNT?, BT:TWS:SCAN:ITEM?
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:SCAN?, BT:TWS:SCAN:COUNT?, BT:TWS:SCAN:ITEM?

The list is cleared when a search starts and holds up to 8 entries; seen counts every well-formed hit of the search (up to 255), so seen above kept means peers were found and dropped for lack of space. BT:TWS:SCAN? returns the whole list in one line and stops appending when the line would overflow, so COUNT? plus ITEM? is the complete form. ITEM? answers :ERR:RANGE for an index at or past kept and :ERR:PARAM for a bad parameter; f1 and f2 are two fields of the module's report whose meaning the vendor does not document.

BT:TWS:SCAN?         ->  BT:TWS:SCAN:2;4142DE0BCDAC,-78,10,Secondary-AMP;AABBCCDDEEFF,-92,2,
BT:TWS:SCAN:COUNT?   ->  BT:TWS:SCAN:COUNT:2,2
BT:TWS:SCAN:ITEM? 0  ->  BT:TWS:SCAN:ITEM:4142DE0BCDAC,-78,10,Secondary-AMP,1,2

docs.title: BT:TWS:SCAN:DIAG?, BT:TWS:PEERDIAG?
docs.text:
Commands: BT:TWS:SCAN:DIAG?, BT:TWS:PEERDIAG?

Two parser diagnostics for support cases: how many report lines of the module arrived, how many were decoded, and the last line as raw hex (at most 64 bytes), because the module's lines can contain bytes that would corrupt a plain answer. Used when a search finds nothing (BT:TWS:SCAN:ITEM? 0 answers ERR:RANGE) or when a streaming pair reports its role as Unknown. The counters reset when a search starts and when the module stops answering.

docs.title: BT:AIO?
docs.text:
PCB 1.4 routes the two LED outputs of the Bluetooth module to the MCU. The firmware samples them every 100 ms (0 = LED on) and counts their edges, which grow while a LED blinks. A bench diagnostic today, reserved for a later TWS feature. BT:AIO:N/A on PCB 1.3.

BT:AIO?  ->  BT:AIO:0,1,0,57

docs.title: BT:AT
docs.text:
Sends the quoted command to the module as it is and returns every line the module emitted during a 500 ms window, hex-encoded (the example answer is OK), at most 6 lines; truncated is 1 when a line or the buffer overflowed. The parameter must be quoted: an unquoted value containing + is cut at the + by the command parser and a different command is sent. The module's own status polling continues, so an unrelated line can land in the window; the answer sought is normally the first. :ERR:PARAM when the argument does not begin with AT, :ERR:MODULE when the module could not be written.

Unfiltered: anything the module accepts is sent, including AT+RESTORE (factory reset of the module) and AT+BAUD (breaks the serial link to the MCU). A development aid, not a product feature.

BT:AT "AT+PEERCONN"  ->  BT:AT:1,0;4F4B

docs.text:
Four fields: manufacturer, model, the serial number of the factory record (N/A on a board without one) and the short firmware version (yy.mm.r, with +dev on a development build). Firmware before 26.10.1 sent a fixed text as the third field.

*IDN?  ->  MURA LABS,JP150,JP150-0001-0021,26.10.1

docs.title: ping
docs.text:
The quickest way to tell a slow module from a dead link: a command the firmware does not know draws no answer at all, while ping always answers.

ping  ->  pong

docs.title: *RST
docs.text:
Answers first, then writes the settings that still wait for their autosave (at most 1 s), and resets at least 100 ms after the answer, so the answer also leaves over USB. A setting changed right before *RST is kept. SYS:RESET:CAUSE? answers SOFTWARE after it.

*RST  ->  Resetting device...

docs.title: DSP: boot memory
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.4since 26.10.1generated2026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF referenceJP150 SCPI Command Reference, revision 1.2 · 4.0 MB

The DSP boot memory of PCB 1.4, a 4 MB SPI flash (W25Q32JV) on the DSP's master port. A multiplexer lets the module reach it while the DSP is held in reset, so every command here needs SYS:POWER:MODE SLEEP or STANDBY first and answers DSP_ACTIVE otherwise. PCB 1.3 boots its DSP from an I2C EEPROM that SigmaStudio writes directly; there the commands answer NO_BUS. DSP: boot memory describes the whole procedure; the bench tool dsp_flash.py and MuraLink implement it with these commands. Error words are NO_BUS, DSP_ACTIVE, BAD_ARGS, BUSY, CRC_ERROR, VERIFY_ERROR and FAILED.

docs.title: DSP:FLASH:BUS?
docs.text:
A diagnostic that checks that the DSP releases the bus in reset. Each field is the level of the line with the module's internal pull-up, then with its pull-down: 10 means the line follows the pulls and nothing drives it. A released bus reads 10,10,10,11 (chip select keeps its own pull-up).

DSP:FLASH:BUS?  ->  DSP:FLASH:BUS:10,10,10,11

docs.title: DSP:FLASH:ID?
docs.text:
The JEDEC identification (manufacturer, type, capacity) and status register 1 of the flash, in hex. The W25Q32JV of PCB 1.4 reads EF4016.

DSP:FLASH:ID?  ->  DSP:FLASH:ID:EF4016,00

docs.title: DSP:FLASH:READ?
docs.text:
Two capital hex digits per byte. An address or length past the end of the 4 MB flash, or a bad parameter, is an SCPI error without an answer, unlike the error words of the other commands. Erased flash reads FF.

DSP:FLASH:READ? 0,16  ->  DSP:FLASH:READ:AA00001000000060006400040000001D

docs.title: DSP:FLASH:ERASE
docs.text:
Both values are multiples of 4096; up to 64 KB per call, which takes up to about 8 s.

DSP:FLASH:ERASE 0,8192  ->  DSP:FLASH:ERASE:OK

docs.title: DSP:FLASH:WRITE
docs.text:
Programs the quoted hex bytes into erased flash without crossing a 256-byte page. crc32 is the CRC-32 of those bytes as a decimal number (zlib's crc32); a mismatch answers CRC_ERROR before anything is programmed. The bytes are read back after programming (VERIFY_ERROR).

DSP:FLASH:WRITE 0,"AA000010",505755161  ->  DSP:FLASH:WRITE:OK

docs.title: DSP:FLASH:CRC?
docs.text:
Eight hex digits, for the host to compare with the CRC-32 of the image it wrote. About 15 us per byte (1 MB in about 16 s), so allow a long timeout. A whole ADAU1452 image (at most about 200 KB) fits in one call; more than 1 MB answers BAD_ARGS.

DSP:FLASH:CRC? 0,2304  ->  DSP:FLASH:CRC:C9053057

The last DSP boot, state and duration – DSP:BOOT:<state>,<ms>,<not_started>,<no_answer> 26.10.1 1.3, 1.4 DSP:SELFBOOT? DSP self boot setting and the level of the SELFBOOT pin – DSP:SELFBOOT:<setting>,<pin> 26.10.1 1.3, 1.4 DSP:SELFBOOT Set the DSP self boot 0, 1 DSP:SELFBOOT:OK 26.10.1 1.3, 1.4

Since is the release the command appeared in; 26.6.2 is the oldest release documented here, so a command marked 26.6.2 may be older.

docs.title: DSP:SETBLOCK
docs.text:
A direct write of one 4-byte value to a parameter address of the DSP program, as SigmaStudio would do it. A diagnostic primitive: parameters that the DSP program manages through its IPAT (the input mux among them) must be written with DSP:IPAT:SETBLOCK, so that the program's own copy stays in step.

DSP:SETBLOCK 100,123456  ->  setblock:100,123456

docs.title: DSP:IPAT:SETBLOCK
docs.text:
Writes one value through the indirect parameter access table (IPAT) of the DSP program. The first parameter is the table's write address of the parameter, from the program's export. Nothing is read back. DSP: parameters over the control interface explains the table.

DSP:IPAT:SETBLOCK 24576,2  ->  ipatsetblock:24576,2

docs.title: DSP:LVLMETER:RMS?
docs.text:
The RMS output of the program's level meter, read through the IPAT: raw is the Q8.24 word (16777216 = full scale), linear is raw / 16777216 with six decimals. The conversion to dB is left to the host. The meter sits before the volume. A read failure is an SCPI error, never a stale value. The automatic power-down compares its threshold with this reading.

DSP:LVLMETER:RMS?  ->  DSP:LVLMETER:RMS:167772,0.010000

docs.title: DSP status bits
docs.text:
Commands: DSP:CORE:START?, DSP:CORE:KILL?, DSP:PLL:LOCK?, DSP:PC:ADVANCING?

Four status bits of the ADAU1452, read live. A running program reads start 1, kill 0, PLL 1, advancing 1. DSP:PC:ADVANCING? answers 1 while the core status is running or sleeping between samples; it no longer samples the program counter, which also moves while no program runs. ERROR while the DSP is in reset or the I2C guard is triggered.

DSP:CORE:START?    ->  DSP:CORE:START:1
DSP:PLL:LOCK?      ->  DSP:PLL:LOCK:1
DSP:PC:ADVANCING?  ->  DSP:PC:ADVANCING:1

docs.title: DSP:CORE:STATUS?
docs.text:
SLEEP is the normal reading of a running program: the core has finished its instructions for this sample and waits for the next one. DSP:CORE:STATUS:ERROR while the DSP is in reset or the I2C guard is triggered.

DSP core states

Value Meaning 0,NOT_RUNNING No program runs 1,RUNNING The core executes instructions 2,PAUSED The core is paused 3,SLEEP The core finished this sample and waits for the next one, the normal reading of a running program 4,STALLED The core is stalled 
DSP:CORE:STATUS?  ->  DSP:CORE:STATUS:3,SLEEP

docs.title: DSP:PANIC?
docs.text:
The ADAU1452's panic manager, read live; both registers stay set until the DSP is reset. After three failed self-boot attempts the core raises a software panic (bit 15, 0x8000). Bits 5 to 7 (0x0020, 0x0040, 0x0080) are data-memory parity flags that the current DSP programs raise at every start on both board revisions, so a non-zero code alone is not a fault. ERROR while the DSP is in reset or the I2C guard is triggered.

DSP:PANIC?  ->  DSP:PANIC:1,0x0080

docs.title: DSP:BOOT?
docs.text:
The last boot of the DSP as the firmware timed it, after power-up and after every wake that released the DSP from reset. The firmware polls the program start bit every 50 ms from 50 ms after the release and then writes the selected input. ms is the time from the release to the poll that found the program started (about 20 ms short after a wake); not_started counts polls that found no program yet, no_answer polls the DSP did not answer. After 5 s without a start the state is FAILED; the bit is then re-read every second, so a program loaded later by SigmaStudio turns the state to READY. Typical: PCB 1.4 READY,53 from its SPI flash, PCB 1.3 READY,252 from its I2C EEPROM; an image whose speed word does not match the boot memory takes about 3 s. A memory read, not subject to the I2C guard.

DSP boot states

Value Meaning WAITING The DSP was released from reset and its program has not started yet READY The program started and the selected input has been written FAILED No start within 5 s; still re-checked every second 
DSP:BOOT?  ->  DSP:BOOT:READY,53,0,0

docs.title: DSP:SELFBOOT
docs.text:
Commands: DSP:SELFBOOT?, DSP:SELFBOOT

Whether the DSP loads its program from its boot memory when it leaves reset. setting is the stored value, pin the level of the SELFBOOT net now; on PCB 1.3 a closed DIP switch holds the pin at 0 whatever the setting. The DSP samples the pin only when it leaves reset, so a change takes effect at the next DSP reset (SYS:POWER:MODE SLEEP and back to NORMAL, or a power cycle); the command does not restart the DSP. With self boot off the DSP loads no program and there is no audio until the setting is 1 again and the DSP is reset: the state SigmaStudio needs to write the boot memory through the DSP. An invalid value is an SCPI error. A stored setting (autosave after 0.1 s).

Default: 1.

DSP:SELFBOOT?   ->  DSP:SELFBOOT:1,1
DSP:SELFBOOT 0  ->  DSP:SELFBOOT:OK

docs.title: System: I2C bus guard
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.4since 26.8.0generated2026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Download the PDF referenceJP150 SCPI Command Reference, revision 1.2 · 4.0 MB

Detection of a SigmaStudio USBi programmer on the DSP's I2C control bus (connector J11). While a second master is active, the firmware stands down from the bus so that a running download is not corrupted: the level-meter LEDs freeze on their last frame and the DSP status queries answer ERROR without touching the bus. The guard does not gate commands that write to the DSP on request: a host suspends its own polling while SYS:I2C:GUARD? reads 1.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Function Parameter Answer Since Boards SYS:I2C:GUARD? A second master is active on the DSP bus – SYS:I2C:GUARD:<0|1> 26.8.0 1.3, 1.4 SYS:I2C:GUARD:COUNT? Programmer episodes since start – SYS:I2C:GUARD:COUNT:<n> 26.8.0 1.3, 1.4 SYS:I2C:GUARD:STUCK? A bus line is held low (hardware fault) – SYS:I2C:GUARD:STUCK:<0|1> 26.8.0 1.3, 1.4

Since is the release the command appeared in; 26.6.2 is the oldest release documented here, so a command marked 26.6.2 may be older.

docs.title: SYS:I2C:GUARD?
docs.text:
1 from the first sample that shows a second master (a SigmaStudio USBi) until 750 ms after the last one; the firmware samples the bus lines at 10 kHz. While 1, the level-meter task skips its DSP read and the DSP status queries answer ERROR without touching the bus. The guard does not gate commands that drive the bus on request (DSP:SETBLOCK, DSP:IPAT:SETBLOCK, DSP:LVLMETER:RMS?, AMPx:CLOCK?, SYS:MEAS:TEMP:PWRSTAGE?): a host suspends its own polling while the guard reads 1. A 0 on its own is ambiguous: the flag is forced to 0 while SYS:I2C:GUARD:STUCK? is 1, so read both.

SYS:I2C:GUARD?  ->  SYS:I2C:GUARD:1

docs.title: SYS:I2C:GUARD:COUNT?
docs.text:
Episodes, not samples: one continuous SigmaStudio download is one episode, and activity inside the 750 ms hold-off extends it. The module's own drivers add an episode when they find the bus busy or lose arbitration (a missing device, which only fails to acknowledge, does not count). Free-running since start, not stored, cleared only by a restart. A non-zero count with SYS:I2C:GUARD? at 0 is the normal state after a SigmaStudio session.

SYS:I2C:GUARD:COUNT?  ->  SYS:I2C:GUARD:COUNT:3

docs.title: SYS:I2C:GUARD:STUCK?
docs.text:
1 when SCL or SDA has been low for 3 s without interruption, far longer than any transaction: a stuck device, a shorted line or an unpowered bus segment, not programmer activity. While 1, the guard stops suppressing the firmware's bus accesses, so that the fault shows through the ordinary error answers of the affected commands. Self-clearing once both lines are high again.

SYS:I2C:GUARD:STUCK?  ->  SYS:I2C:GUARD:STUCK:0

What the module is and how it started: the firmware version and the installed package, the factory record of the board, the MCU, uptime, the cause of the last reset, the health of the real-time kernel, how the bootloader started the firmware, the protection state of the microcontroller, and the command that restarts the module into update mode.

docs.text:
