Since is the release the command appeared in; 26.6.2 is the oldest release documented here, so a command marked 26.6.2 may be older. †: also served in the safe state (see SYS:BOARD:TYPE?).

docs.title: SYS:VERSION?
docs.text: A release build answers <version> (release) built <yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm> [<commit>], a development build <version>+dev.<n>.g<commit> (branch <name>[, dirty]) built <date>. The short version alone is the fourth field of *IDN?.

docs.title: SYS:FW:PACKAGE?
docs.text:
Read from the header of the running image. variant is RELEASE, SPECIAL or DEVELOPMENT (UNKNOWN for a value this firmware does not know); label names a special build, otherwise empty; counter is the security counter the bootloader compares with its rollback floor; key is PROD or DEV. SYS:FW:PACKAGE:NONE when the image carries no valid header, for example a debugger load without the post-build step. MuraLink shows the answer next to the version and checks it before an update.

SYS:FW:PACKAGE?  ->  SYS:FW:PACKAGE:RELEASE,,1,PROD
SYS:FW:PACKAGE?  ->  SYS:FW:PACKAGE:SPECIAL,ACME-01,1,PROD

docs.title: SYS:MCU:TYPE?, SYS:MCU:REV?
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:MCU:TYPE?, SYS:MCU:REV?

Decoded from the device identification registers of the STM32.

MCU revisions

Value Meaning Z Revision Z B Revision B 1_OR_C Revision 1 or C UNKNOWN A revision identifier the firmware does not know 
SYS:MCU:TYPE?  ->  SYS:MCU:TYPE:STM32F412XX
SYS:MCU:REV?   ->  SYS:MCU:REV:B

docs.title: SYS:BOARD:ID
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:BOARD:ID?, SYS:BOARD:ID

The query reports the factory record in the one-time-programmable memory (OTP) when there is one, otherwise the identity written with the setter into the flash record, otherwise N/A fields. On a board with a factory record the setter answers LOCKED and writes nothing: the record cannot be rewritten. Without one it writes both strings (1 to 16 printable characters each, no spaces) to the flash record synchronously: OK confirms the write, ERROR a failed one; invalid parameters are an SCPI error. Every unit that leaves the factory carries a factory record, so the setter is a service command.

SYS:BOARD:ID?                     ->  SYS:BOARD:ID:1.4,JP150-0001-0021
SYS:BOARD:ID "1.3","JP150_0024"   ->  SYS:BOARD:ID:LOCKED

docs.title: SYS:BOARD:REV?, SYS:BOARD:SERIAL?
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:BOARD:REV?, SYS:BOARD:SERIAL?

The two halves of SYS:BOARD:ID?. The factory record wins over the flash record; N/A when neither exists. A factory serial number reads <product>-<batch>-<unit> with at least four digits per number.

SYS:BOARD:REV?     ->  SYS:BOARD:REV:1.4
SYS:BOARD:SERIAL?  ->  SYS:BOARD:SERIAL:JP150-0001-0021

docs.title: SYS:BOARD:RECORD?
docs.text:
The identity written once per board at the factory into the OTP memory of the microcontroller; the firmware reads it once at start. block is the OTP block that holds the record (0 to 11): a correction made at the factory appears with a higher block. NONE on a board without a valid record. Read-only: nothing in the firmware writes OTP.

SYS:BOARD:RECORD?  ->  SYS:BOARD:RECORD:OTP,JP150,1.4,JP150-0001-0021,2026-10-02,0
SYS:BOARD:RECORD?  ->  SYS:BOARD:RECORD:NONE

docs.title: SYS:BOARD:TYPE?
docs.text:
The firmware identifies the board only from the factory record: PCB 1.3 and 1.4 differ in the bus the DSP is on, its clock source and several pins, and nothing else tells them apart. A board it does not support starts in the safe state: the DSP and both power stages stay in reset, the status LED shows the pattern described under Indicators, and only the commands marked with a dagger on these pages are served. Every other command answers the line ERR:BOARD:UNSUPPORTED without a prefix, at once, so a host learns that the command exists but is not available. The safe state exists so that such a board can still be identified and updated to a firmware that supports it.

Board types

Value Meaning JP150-1.3 JP150, PCB 1.3 JP150-1.4 JP150, PCB 1.4 UNSUPPORTED,NO_RECORD No valid factory record; the board is not provisioned (safe state) UNSUPPORTED,PRODUCT The record names another product (safe state) UNSUPPORTED,REVISION The record names a JP150 revision this firmware does not support (safe state) 
SYS:BOARD:TYPE?  ->  SYS:BOARD:TYPE:JP150-1.4
SYS:BOARD:TYPE?  ->  SYS:BOARD:TYPE:UNSUPPORTED,NO_RECORD

docs.title: SYS:UPTIME?, SYS:RUNTIME:TOTAL?
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:UPTIME?, SYS:RUNTIME:TOTAL?

Not yet a real counter: the answer is the uptime plus a fixed offset of 42 days. A persisted total runtime is planned; until then do not display the value as a fact.

SYS:UPTIME?  ->  SYS:UPTIME:0001:12:34:56

docs.title: SYS:RESET:CAUSE?
docs.text:
Decoded once at start and kept, so every read of one session gives the same answer. When the bootloader started the firmware, the cause comes from the reset flags the bootloader captured. IWDG after a watchdog reset is the one to watch for in a support case.

Reset causes

Value Meaning POWERON Power-on or power-down reset BROWNOUT Brown-out reset without a power-on EXTERNAL The reset pin only, for example a debugger reset SOFTWARE A software reset: *RST, SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS, the bootloader's return from update mode IWDG The independent watchdog; a monitored firmware task stopped making progress WWDG The window watchdog (not used by the firmware) LOWPOWER Low-power management reset UNKNOWN No reset flag was set 
SYS:RESET:CAUSE?  ->  SYS:RESET:CAUSE:POWERON

docs.title: SYS:RTOS?
docs.text:
Heap figures in bytes, live. tasks_not_created is counted once at start over every task the firmware creates: a value above 0 means a feature is silently missing, and is worth a support report.

SYS:RTOS?  ->  SYS:RTOS:3576,3576,0

docs.title: SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO?
docs.text:
started is YES when the bootloader handed over in this start, NO for a direct start (a debug session); config PROD or DEV (NONE with NO); version the bootloader version word; attempt numbers this start since the last confirmed one, 1 meaning the previous start confirmed itself (after three unconfirmed starts the bootloader enters update mode instead of starting the firmware). floor is the rollback floor, the lowest security counter the bootloader still installs; it only rises. The last five fields describe the latest update attempt: its result and cause as codes (tables below), the firmware version word before and in the package, and the attempt number over the module's life. A version word is yy << 24 | mm << 16 | r: 0x1A0A0001 is 26.10.1. Firmware before 26.10.1 sends only the first four fields; later firmware may append more, so a host reads the fields it knows.

The query is deliberately not SYS:BOOTLOADER?: without its ? that is the command that restarts the module into update mode.

Update results (update_result)

Code Meaning 0 No attempt recorded 1 Installed and verified 2 Refused before the firmware slot was modified; the installed firmware is unchanged 3 Ended with an error after the slot was modified; the module had no valid firmware until the next installation 4 Did not finish: host abort, USB reset, idle timeout, or a reset or power loss during the attempt 5 Begun and not finished; the bootloader settles such an entry at its next start

Update causes (update_cause)

Code Meaning 0 No cause: a successful attempt, or none recorded 1 Unknown package format 2 Package of the other configuration (a development package on a production unit, or the reverse) 3 Package failed verification 4 Package for other hardware 5 Image larger than the firmware slot 6 Security counter below the rollback floor 7 A digest does not match: the package is damaged 8 Erase, program or read-back of the flash failed 9 Block out of sequence, or the transfer ended before the whole package 10 No data from the host for 30 s 11 DFU abort or USB reset by the host 12 Reset or power loss during the attempt, found at the next start 
SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO?  ->  SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO:YES,PROD,0x00000000,1,1,1,0,0x1A080000,0x1A0A0001,9

docs.title: SYS:BOOTLOADER
docs.text:
Mutes the power stages, writes pending settings (at most 1 s), leaves an update request for the bootloader, answers, and restarts the module 500 ms later. The serial port disappears and the DFU device of the update mode (USB 16D0:15B7) appears. Without a transfer the module returns to its firmware after 5 minutes. How an update works describes the mode.

SYS:BOOTLOADER  ->  SYS:BOOTLOADER:OK

docs.title: SYS:PROTECTION?
docs.text:
The protection state of the microcontroller's option bytes, read-only: rdp the read-out protection level 0, 1 or 2; wrp_bl 1 when the bootloader's flash sectors are write-protected; bor the brown-out reset level 0 (off) to 3; sprmod the write-protection mode bit. A production unit answers 2,1,3,0. Diagnostics for support; nothing in the firmware depends on it.

SYS:PROTECTION?  ->  SYS:PROTECTION:2,1,3,0

docs.title: SYS:PERFTEST
docs.text:
Echoes its parameter, for round-trip timing of the link.

SYS:PERFTEST hello  ->  SYS:PERFTEST:hello

The selected audio input and the enable mask that decides which inputs the volume encoder cycles through. Both are stored settings.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Function Parameter Answer Since Boards SYS:INPUT? Selected input – SYS:INPUT:<source> 26.6.2 1.3, 1.4 SYS:INPUT Select an input <source> SYS:INPUT:<OK|ERR:DISABLED|ERR:PARAM> 26.6.2 1.3, 1.4 SYS:INPUT:ENABLE? Whether an input is enabled <source> SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:<source>:<0|1> 26.8.0 1.3, 1.4 SYS:INPUT:ENABLE Enable or disable an input <source>,<0|1> SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:<OK|ERR:LAST|ERR:PARAM> 26.8.0 1.3, 1.4 SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:LIST? docs.title: SYS:INPUT
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:INPUT?, SYS:INPUT

The setter switches only to an enabled source (SYS:INPUT:ENABLE) and answers OK; a disabled source is refused with ERR:DISABLED and the input stays as it was. ERR:PARAM is a word that is not a source; an argument that cannot be parsed at all is an SCPI error without an answer. The query reports the source the firmware last wrote to the DSP, which after a start or a wake is the stored selection. SYS:INPUT:NONE is a defensive answer for a state that the commands and the encoder cannot reach. The selected input is a stored setting (autosave after 2 s).

The encoder button cycles through the enabled inputs in the order USB, BT, SPDIF, I2S, SINE, WIFI. SYS:INPUT is a prefix of the SYS:INPUT:ENABLE commands, and the setter's answers share the prefix of the query's answer: a response matcher must not read them as a source.

Input sources

Value Meaning BT Bluetooth I2S The I2S input connector SINE The DSP's built-in test tone WIFI The Wi-Fi module USB USB audio SPDIF S/PDIF 
SYS:INPUT?     ->  SYS:INPUT:BT
SYS:INPUT USB  ->  SYS:INPUT:OK
SYS:INPUT I2S  ->  SYS:INPUT:ERR:DISABLED

docs.title: SYS:INPUT:ENABLE
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:INPUT:ENABLE?, SYS:INPUT:ENABLE

A disabled input is skipped by the encoder and refused by SYS:INPUT. The last enabled input cannot be disabled: the request answers ERR:LAST and nothing changes, so there is always a selectable source. Disabling the input that is selected switches the module to the next enabled source in the encoder's order before the answer is sent, so a host re-reads SYS:INPUT? after it. The mask is a stored setting (autosave after 1 s); a stored selection that is disabled at start is replaced by the next enabled source before the DSP is written.

Default: all inputs enabled.

SYS:INPUT:ENABLE? BT    ->  SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:BT:1
SYS:INPUT:ENABLE SINE,0 ->  SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:OK

docs.title: SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:LIST?
docs.text:
Every enabled source in the order BT, I2S, SINE, WIFI, USB, SPDIF (not the encoder's order), never empty. A source absent from the list is disabled.

SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:LIST?  ->  SYS:INPUT:ENABLE:LIST:BT,I2S,WIFI,USB

docs.title: SYS:MEAS:VOLT?, SYS:MEAS:CURR?, SYS:MEAS:POW?
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:MEAS:VOLT?, SYS:MEAS:CURR?, SYS:MEAS:POW?

Two decimals each. On PCB 1.4 the three come from the INA226 power monitor: the voltage after the inrush limiter and the shunt (slightly below the supply input, 0 to 36 V), the whole-board current with 0.625 mA resolution, averaged, a new result about every 141 ms; when the monitor cannot be read the queries draw no answer (an SCPI error). On PCB 1.3 the voltage comes from the ADC and the current from the TMCS1108 sensor through the ADC with an 80 ms filter. SYS:MEAS:POW? multiplies voltage and current of one reading; the product of separate VOLT? and CURR? answers can differ while the load changes with the music.

SYS:MEAS:VOLT?  ->  SYS:MEAS:VOLT:24.50
SYS:MEAS:CURR?  ->  SYS:MEAS:CURR:1.25
SYS:MEAS:POW?   ->  SYS:MEAS:POW:30.63

docs.text:
Commands: SYS:MEAS:TEMP?, SYS:MEAS:TEMP:MCU?, SYS:MEAS:TEMP:MCU:MIN?, SYS:MEAS:TEMP:MCU:MAX?

The temperature sensor inside the STM32; SYS:MEAS:TEMP? is the same value with a shorter prefix, kept for compatibility. The minimum and maximum are the extremes of the readings taken at query time: every MCU temperature query folds a fresh reading into them, nothing is sampled between queries, and the values do not survive a restart.

docs.text:
Commands: SYS:MEAS:TEMP:PWRSTAGE?, SYS:MEAS:TEMP:PWRSTAGE:MIN?, SYS:MEAS:TEMP:PWRSTAGE:MAX?

The TMP112 sensor on the power-stage heatsink, read over I2C on request (-40 to 125 degrees C). A missing sensor or a bus error is an SCPI error, never a made-up value. The minimum and maximum follow the same query-time rule as the MCU extremes and answer an SCPI error until the sensor has been read once.

docs.title: SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE?
docs.text:
Recorded once at start; it does not change while the module runs. OK and NODATA mean the autosave works. After ABSENT or ERROR nothing is saved in this session, and SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING? always answers 0: a host takes persistence from this query and never reports a setting as saved after ABSENT or ERROR.

Settings-memory states

Value Meaning OK The settings were restored from the EEPROM NODATA The EEPROM was empty or held an older layout; defaults and the flash backup are in use and the autosave fills it ABSENT The EEPROM did not answer at start; nothing is autosaved in this session ERROR An I2C or layout error at start; nothing is autosaved in this session 
SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE?  ->  SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE:OK

docs.title: SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING?
docs.text:
1 while at least one setting waits for its autosave debounce or is being written, 0 when nothing is outstanding. Commands run in order and every autosaved setter marks its write before it answers, so a query sent right after a setter already sees it. The 1 lasts the setting's debounce (0.1 s for DSP:SELFBOOT and the trigger settings, 1 s for the input enable flags and the TWS fallback role, 2 s for the input, 3 s for the volumes, 5 s for the automatic power-down settings) plus up to 0.5 s: at most about 5.5 s after the last change. Changes the host did not make show too: the encoder, the volume from the Wi-Fi module, the autosave's own re-check every 10 minutes, and the first writes after a start that found empty slots.

0 is not proof of success: a write that fails three times in a row is given up and also ends at 0 (the 10-minute re-check tries again), and without a working EEPROM the answer is always 0. The answer has one field today; later firmware may append fields after it. *RST and SYS:BOOTLOADER write pending settings before they restart the module.

AMP:VOL 40
SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING?  ->  SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING:1
(3 to 3.5 s later)
SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING?  ->  SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING:0

docs.title: SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS
docs.text:
Returns the user settings to their defaults: the master and channel volumes, the input enable mask, the automatic power-down settings, the DSP self boot and the three trigger settings. The selected input, the TWS fallback role, the board identity, the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi pairings and the DSP program are kept. In order: the power stages are muted, every setting gets its default, the autosave writes them (at most 1 s), the flash backup record is rewritten, the answer is sent, and 500 ms after the answer the module restarts, also after an ERR:* answer. The defaults take effect through the normal start-up; the outputs stay muted until then.

OK: every write was confirmed. ERR:EEPROM: an EEPROM write was not confirmed within 1 s or was given up. ERR:FLASH: the EEPROM writes were confirmed but the flash record could not be written. After an error the reset may be partial, so a host re-reads the settings after it reconnects. The answer can take about 2.2 s (a flash sector erase of up to 1.1 s, during which the module does not respond), so a host waits 4 s or more for it. SYS:RESET:CAUSE? answers SOFTWARE after the restart. Not served in the safe state.

SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS  ->  SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS:OK
(the module restarts 500 ms later)

docs.title: The flash backup record
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:NVM:FLASH:SAVE, SYS:NVM:FLASH:LOAD, SYS:NVM:FLASH:ERASE, SYS:NVM:FLASH:CHECK?

Service commands for the flash record that backs up the volumes, the selected input, the TWS fallback role and the board identity written with SYS:BOARD:ID. SAVE writes the record (skipped when nothing changed; when the sector is full it is erased first, which stalls the module for 1 to 2 s). LOAD restores the record into the running settings, NO_DATA when there is none. ERASE clears the sector; it does not reset the settings, because their EEPROM copy wins at the next start: use SYS:NVM:DEFAULTS for that. CHECK? answers the sequence number of the last valid record, 4294967295 when there is none; it rises by one with every write.

SYS:NVM:FLASH:CHECK?  ->  SYS:NVM:FLASH:CHECK:42

docs.title: SYS:POWER:MODE
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:POWER:MODE?, SYS:POWER:MODE

Each level switches off one more part of the module than the previous one:

Level Power stages 12 V rail 5 V rail DSP NORMAL on on on running PWRSTAGE_IDLE muted, in reset on on running PWRSTAGE_OFF muted, in reset off on running SLEEP muted, in reset off on in reset STANDBY muted, in reset off off in reset

The MCU keeps running and answering in every level. The level is not stored: the module starts in NORMAL. Returning to NORMAL from PWRSTAGE_OFF, SLEEP or STANDBY re-initialises the power stages before they are unmuted; the control interface waits for about 350 ms plus that initialisation, so a host allows for it in its timeout. Leaving SLEEP or STANDBY boots the DSP from its boot memory again, and the firmware re-applies the selected input itself. In STANDBY the Wi-Fi module is unpowered: WIFI:* queries fail or time out then, which is not a lost connection. Automatic power-down, the 12 V trigger and audio wake change the level without a command; SYS:POWER:AUTO:STATE? and SYS:TRIG? show why.

Power levels

Value Meaning NORMAL Everything on PWRSTAGE_IDLE The power stages are muted and held in reset; their 12 V supply stays on PWRSTAGE_OFF As PWRSTAGE_IDLE, and the 12 V supply of the power stages is off SLEEP As PWRSTAGE_OFF, and the DSP is held in reset. The 5 V rail, and with it the Wi-Fi module, stays powered STANDBY As SLEEP, and the 5 V rail is off, so the Wi-Fi module is unpowered. The MCU keeps running and answering 
SYS:POWER:MODE?       ->  SYS:POWER:MODE:NORMAL
SYS:POWER:MODE SLEEP

docs.text:

docs.title: SYS:POWER:AUTO
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:POWER:AUTO?, SYS:POWER:AUTO

The master switch of the automatic power-down after silence. Off by default; a stored setting. A value above 1 is an SCPI error.

Default: 0.

docs.title: SYS:POWER:AUTO:MODE
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:POWER:AUTO:MODE?, SYS:POWER:AUTO:MODE

NORMAL is refused with an SCPI error: it is the level being left. The setting is a preference: the level actually entered is limited at the moment of the transition, for example to SLEEP while Wi-Fi is the selected input, because the Wi-Fi module must stay powered to wake the module on audio. SYS:POWER:AUTO:STATE? reports both the configured and the effective level. A stored setting.

Default: PWRSTAGE_OFF.

docs.title: SYS:POWER:AUTO:DELAY
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:POWER:AUTO:DELAY?, SYS:POWER:AUTO:DELAY

Whole seconds of continuous silence before the module powers down. Values below 10 s are refused: shorter than that, the module could power down in a gap between tracks. A stored setting.

Default: 1800.

docs.title: SYS:POWER:AUTO:THRESHOLD
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:POWER:AUTO:THRESHOLD?, SYS:POWER:AUTO:THRESHOLD

The threshold is in the raw units of DSP:LVLMETER:RMS? (Q8.24: 16777216 is full scale), not in dB; dBFS = 20 log10(raw / 16777216). The meter sits before the volume, so the threshold is a source-level one, unaffected by volume or mute. The default of 5 (about -130 dBFS) is near the floor on purpose: every input is digital, a stopped stream reads exactly 0 and anything playing clears 5 by orders of magnitude. Residuals in the DSP chain (dither, a DC offset, a decaying RMS detector) also count as audio and postpone the power-down; raise the threshold if the module does not power down. Reference points: 11879 is -63 dBFS (the bottom LED of the level meter), 2112126 is -18 dBFS (loud programme material). 0 means nothing ever counts as silence; a value above 16777216 would make everything count as silence, so that the module powers down during playback and cannot wake on audio. MuraLink refuses such values; the command itself does not. A stored setting.

Default: 5.

docs.title: SYS:POWER:AUTO:STATE?
docs.text:
Everything a host needs to show a countdown: enabled mirrors SYS:POWER:AUTO?; armed is 1 while silence is being counted, that is enabled and in NORMAL; configured and effective are the set and the limited target level; then the delay, the silence so far and the remaining seconds. The elapsed time restarts at 0 on every level change, so a wake always gets the full delay. With armed 0 the last two fields mean nothing.

SYS:POWER:AUTO:STATE?  ->  SYS:POWER:AUTO:STATE:1,1,STANDBY,SLEEP,1800,412,1388

docs.title: SYS:TRIG:MODE
docs.text:
Commands: SYS:TRIG:MODE?, SYS:TRIG:MODE

OFF ignores the input. FOLLOW: a change to high returns the module to NORMAL, a change to low takes it to the target level; the level found at start counts too, so a module started without a trigger powers down about 5 s after start, and so does a switch to FOLLOW (the current level applies once). The encoder and the commands can still change the level until the trigger changes again. ONOFF: the input is a push button; a press while powered down wakes the module, a press that begins in NORMAL and is held for 1 s powers down to the target level. The press that wakes never powers down, and the level found at start is not a press. An invalid value is an SCPI error. A stored setting (autosave after 0.1 s).

Default: OFF.

FOLLOW mode only. With 1 the automatic decisions never contradict the trigger: no silence power-down while the trigger is high, no audio wake while it is low. With 0 automatic power-down and audio wake work as before, beside the trigger. A stored setting.

Default: 1.

docs.title: First power-up
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

From an unpacked module to the first sound. The module ships with its firmware and the default DSP program installed, so nothing has to be programmed first.

docs.title: Before you switch on
docs.text:
1. Supply. Either a DC supply of 15 to 36 V on POWER IN: pin 1 GND, pin 2 positive, the polarity is protected and the inrush is limited; or a USB Power Delivery source on USB C PD, up to 100 W. Never exceed 36 V (Specifications). With both connected the module selects its supply itself.
  2. Speakers on the four screw terminals AMP0 OUT A, AMP0 OUT B, AMP1 OUT A and AMP1 OUT B, each with its + and − pin marked. The bridging options and the load the power stages accept are on Configuration and Specifications.
  3. A source, for the first sound preferably a phone over Bluetooth, which needs no cable, or a PC on USB DATA (the USB-C connector or the 3-pin header) with a USB-C data cable.
  4. Optionally the encoder on ROTARY ENCODER and a USB-C data cable to the PC for MuraLink. The pinouts are on Connectors and pinouts.

docs.title: What you see at power-up
docs.text:
Indicator Expected If not Power LED A low level with a short bright blip once a second: the firmware runs No light: the supply. A blip every two seconds: the module is in a power-down level; a turn or a press of the encoder wakes it Status LED The colour of the selected input: blue Bluetooth, white Wi-Fi, magenta USB, cyan I2S, amber S/PDIF, yellow test tone Red with a dim white step every second: the safe state. Amber patterns: update mode DSP LED Flashing (1 Hz with the default program): the DSP program runs Dark: no program in the boot memory, or the module sleeps; see Writing the boot memory Level meter Follows the signal of the selected input Stays dark with music playing: the input is not the one that plays, or the module is in a power-down level

The whole table is explained on Indicators and LEDs. The firmware answers at once; the DSP program loads within a quarter of a second (Start-up).

docs.title: The first sound
docs.text:
1. Select the input. Press the encoder button to cycle through the enabled inputs, or click the input in MuraLink. The status LED shows the selection by colour; only enabled inputs are offered (Inputs and the enable mask).
  2. Bluetooth: with the status LED blue, connect from the phone's Bluetooth settings and start playback (Connect a phone). USB: with the status LED magenta, the PC sees a USB audio device named MURA LABS JP150; no driver is needed. Select it as the output device and play. Wi-Fi: needs the one-time network setup first (Wi-Fi setup).
  3. Volume. Turn the encoder, or use the master volume in MuraLink (0 to 99). The volume is saved automatically a few seconds after the last change and restored at the next power-up (Volume and encoder).

docs.title: If nothing plays
docs.text:
• The selected input is the one your source plays to, and it is enabled.
  • The volume is not 0 and the power stages are not muted (MuraLink: Power stage > Controls).
  • The DSP LED flashes. A dark DSP LED with the power LED alive means no DSP program is running.
  • On PCB 1.4 no red FAULT LED is lit next to a power stage; a yellow CLIP LED is only a level warning.
  • The module is in its NORMAL power level, not powered down by the automatic power-down or, on PCB 1.4, by the 12 V trigger (Power levels).
  • The status LED is not red with a white step (safe state) and shows no update pattern.

Troubleshooting continues from here, symptom by symptom.

docs.title: Install MuraLink
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-04Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

MuraLink is the Windows application for the module: every setting, the diagnostics and the firmware update in one window. The short path; the full page is MuraLink: Install.

  1. Download MuraLink_26.10.1.zip from Downloads. It is a zip of about 67 MB; there is no installer, and nothing else has to be installed: the .NET runtime is inside the executable. Unzip it into a folder of your own (MuraLink writes its log files next to the executable).
  2. Run MuraLink_26.10.1.exe. Windows SmartScreen may warn about a program downloaded for the first time: choose More info and Run anyway.
  3. Connect the module with a USB-C data cable to USB DATA (the USB-C connector or the 3-pin header). Windows installs no driver: the module appears as a COM port (Device Manager, Ports). Charge-only cables do not work.
  4. In MuraLink choose that COM port and click Connect. The Overview shows the inputs with the active one highlighted, the master volume and the level meter, the health values (supply, temperatures) and the device line with the model, the board revision and the firmware version.
The Device connection dialog: choose the port and click Connect.

The next step is Check for updates. MuraLink works with every firmware release from 26.6.2 on and shows n/a for what an older firmware cannot report (Firmware compatibility).

docs.title: What to include in a support request
docs.text:
The more of this comes with the first message, the faster the answer:

  1. The identity of the module. *IDN? in one line gives the model, the serial number and the firmware version, for example MURA LABS,JP150,JP150-0001-0021,26.10.1. MuraLink shows the same on Device > Status; the serial number is also on the factory record (SYS:BOARD:RECORD?).
  2. The board. SYS:BOARD:TYPE? (JP150-1.3, JP150-1.4, or UNSUPPORTED,...).
  3. The diagnostics. The answers of SYS:VERSION?, SYS:FW:PACKAGE?, SYS:RESET:CAUSE?, SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO?, SYS:RTOS?, SYS:NVM:EEPROM:STATE? and, for a DSP problem, DSP:BOOT? and DSP:CORE:STATUS?. MuraLink shows them on Diagnostics > System and Software; a copy of both pages is enough.
  4. MuraLink's log. The file Logs/dsp-amp-YYYYMMDD.log next to the executable, or the text of Diagnostics > Log, from the session in which the problem occurred.
  5. What happened. The symptom, what was connected, what you did last, and whether a power cycle changes it. For a firmware update: the message MuraLink showed.
  6. Photos or a short video help with LED patterns and wiring questions.

Please do not send a module back before support has asked for it. The troubleshooting page covers the symptoms that need no support case.

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text:
JP150PCB 1.3PCB 1.42026-11-02Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Do I have to update the firmware? No. A module keeps working on the release it has. The release notes say what a newer release changes and which known issues it fixes; update when one of them matters to you. Check for updates shows how.

Does an update keep my settings and my DSP program? Yes. The settings are kept (the first start after an update from 26.8.0 rebuilds some of them once, see Release 26.10.1). The DSP program is kept unless you choose to write the default program during the update; MuraLink asks, and nothing is preselected.

Can I go back to an older firmware? Only down to the module's rollback floor: the bootloader refuses a package whose security counter is below the floor, which only rises. The floor is shown by MuraLink and SYS:BOOTLOADER:INFO? (How updates work).

Can PCB 1.3 and PCB 1.4 run the same firmware? Yes, from 26.10.1 on, one firmware serves both; the module configures itself from its factory record. A PCB 1.3 module that still runs 26.8.0 cannot take an update bundle by itself; its first update is arranged with support.

Can I write my own DSP program? Yes, with SigmaStudio 4.7 from the starter project. Keep its INPUTS_PROCESSING board, which carries the input mux and the level meter the firmware uses (IPAT and parameters), and write the result into the boot memory of your board revision (Writing the boot memory).

Where is the DIP switch on PCB 1.4? There is none. The DSP self boot is a setting (DSP:SELFBOOT), the master clock is selected by the firmware, and the MCU boot pin is a solder jumper for service (Configuration).

Why does the module not power down on silence? The automatic power-down is off by default (SYS:POWER:AUTO), and a residual signal above the threshold counts as audio. Auto power-down explains the delay, the threshold and the target level; on PCB 1.4 a 12 V trigger with priority can also keep the module awake.

Why does Wi-Fi stop answering in standby? STANDBY is the only level that removes power from the Wi-Fi module. SLEEP keeps it powered, so the module stays reachable on the network and wakes when you play to it (Power levels).

Can two modules play together? Yes, as a True Wireless Stereo pair over Bluetooth: one is the Primary the phone connects to, the other the Secondary. Both units play the full stereo signal; a channel split is done in the DSP program (TWS: about and terms).

Can I control the module from my own software? Yes. The control interface speaks a plain-text command set over the USB virtual COM port and over UART1; the whole set is in the command reference and the rules on the Protocol page. MuraLink uses nothing else.

Where do I find the serial number? *IDN? answers it as its third field, for example JP150-0001-0021; MuraLink shows it on Device > Status. It is the serial number of the factory record, written once at production.

What does a red status LED mean? A red LED with a dim white step every second is the safe state: the firmware does not support the board's factory record. A plain red blink is a fatal error. Both are on Indicators and LEDs.

Do I need a driver for USB? No. The module is a USB audio device and a virtual COM port with the drivers Windows, macOS and Linux bring along. The update mode is a DFU device that MuraLink talks to directly.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
JP1502026-11-05Jan PřibyslavskýThis page does not apply to the product or PCB revision chosen in the header.

Term Meaning Autosave The firmware writes a changed setting to the settings memory a few seconds after the last change. SYS:NVM:EEPROM:PENDING? shows a pending write; MuraLink's footer says Saving... and Settings saved. See Settings and memory. Board record, factory record The product, PCB revision, serial number and production date written once into the module at provisioning. SYS:BOARD:RECORD? shows it; *IDN? reports its serial number. Boot memory The memory the DSP loads its program from at power-up: an I2C EEPROM on PCB 1.3, an SPI flash on PCB 1.4. Boot outcome In TWS, what the last start did with the remembered peer: NoPeer, Reconnected or PeerUnreachable (BT:TWS:BOOTOUTCOME?). Bootloader The module's own bootloader (from 26.10.1) that installs the update packages MuraLink sends and checks the firmware at every start. BTL, PBTL Bridge-tied load, the normal two-channel output of a TAS3251; parallel BTL, both outputs in parallel for one channel with double the current. Default DSP program The basic passthrough design the module ships with, written at the factory and carried in the update bundle for PCB 1.4. The starter project is its source. DFU The USB device class of the bootloader's update mode (16D0:15B7). MuraLink talks to it directly; no driver is needed. E2Prom.Hex SigmaStudio's self-boot export: the image that is written into the boot memory. Enable mask Which of the six inputs can be selected. Encoder The optional rotary control with push button on the ROTARY ENCODER connector: volume, input, wake, and the entry into update mode when held at power-up. Fallback Role In TWS, the role a unit takes at power-up when it remembers no peer: Standalone, Primary or Secondary. Firmware version yy.mm.r: year, month and a counter within the month, for example 26.10.1. +dev marks a development build. Host The Bluetooth audio source, such as a phone. I2C guard, programmer detection The firmware's detection of a SigmaStudio USBi on the DSP bus; while one is active the firmware stands down from the bus (SYS:I2C:GUARD?). IPAT The indirect parameter access table of the DSP program, through which the firmware and the hosts address DSP parameters independently of the program's compiled addresses. Level meter The six-LED bar fed by the DSP program's RMS meter, ahead of the volume control; the same reading drives the silence threshold. Limited mode MuraLink on a module in the safe state: a banner, polling reduced to the available commands, the firmware update still possible. MuraLink The Windows control application for the JP-series modules. OTP The one-time programmable memory of the microcontroller that holds the factory record. Package variant What SYS:FW:PACKAGE? reports about the installed firmware: RELEASE, SPECIAL (with a label) or DEVELOPMENT. Owners run release builds. Peer In TWS, the other unit of the pair. Power level One of NORMAL, PWRSTAGE_IDLE, PWRSTAGE_OFF, SLEEP, STANDBY. Primary, Secondary The TWS unit the host connects to, and the unit that receives the audio from it. Rollback floor The lowest security counter the bootloader still installs; it only rises, so an older release cannot be installed below it. Safe state The state a module starts in when its board record is missing or unsupported: outputs muted, reduced command set, updates possible. SCPI The ASCII command style of the control interface (SYS:INPUT?). Security counter A number in every update package; a package whose counter is below the module's rollback floor is refused. Self boot The DSP loading its program from the boot memory when it leaves reset. A stored setting, on by default (DSP:SELFBOOT); on PCB 1.3 DIP switch 1 set to ON switches it off. SigmaStudio Analog Devices' development environment for the ADAU1452; version 4.7 for the JP150. Silence threshold The level-meter value below which the automatic power-down counts silence (SYS:POWER:AUTO:THRESHOLD). Starter project The SigmaStudio project the module ships with, the base of every own design. Trigger, 12 V trigger The input of PCB 1.4 that switches the module between NORMAL and a power-down level from an external device or a push button. TWS True Wireless Stereo: two units playing one host's audio in sync. Update bundle The published file of a release, JPx_Update_<version>.zip, that MuraLink installs. Update mode The state in which the bootloader waits for an update over USB; status LED amber. USBi The Analog Devices USB programmer for SigmaStudio. Wake on audio Leaving a power-down level when the selected input carries a signal again, part of the automatic power-down. Watchdog The supervision of every firmware task; a module that stops responding restarts itself, and SYS:RESET:CAUSE? then answers IWDG.

Download the PDF guideJP150 Firmware Update, revision 2.0 · 587 kB

From firmware 26.10.1 the module updates itself through its own bootloader: MuraLink hands it the firmware from the update bundle, the module installs it and restarts. No driver, no DIP switch, no separate updater. The update takes about a minute.

  • How updates work

    The update bundle, what the bootloader does, update mode and the USB identity.

  • Update with MuraLink

  • LED indication

    What the status LED and the level meter show during an update.

Which release do I have?

docs.title: The update bundle
docs.text: A release is published as one file, JPx_Update_<version>.zip. It holds the firmware update package, the default DSP program for the boards whose boot memory MuraLink can write (PCB 1.4), the release notes, and a manifest that names the boards the firmware supports. MuraLink reads the bundle in place and checks every file against the manifest before it sends anything to a module. The bundle contains nothing secret and may be passed on.

docs.title: What the bootloader does
docs.text:
• Installs only MURA LABS firmware. The bootloader checks every package before it changes anything, and the installed firmware is verified before it is marked valid.
  • Checks the firmware at every start. A firmware that fails the check is not started; the module waits in update mode instead.
  • Refuses downgrades below the floor. Every package carries a security counter. A package below the module's floor is refused, so a withdrawn release cannot be reinstalled; ordinary older releases remain installable.
  • Survives interruptions. A pulled cable or a power loss at any point leaves the module in update mode with the update ready to be repeated. There is no half-installed state that starts.
  • Keeps the settings. Pending settings are written before the module restarts into update mode.

On a production module the update bundle is the only way to change the firmware; the ST ROM bootloader and the old FirmwareUpdater are not used any more.

docs.title: Update mode
docs.text:
The module enters update mode:

  • when MuraLink sends SYS:BOOTLOADER at the start of an update (the module returns to its firmware by itself after 5 minutes if no update follows);
  • when there is no valid firmware, for example after an interrupted update;
  • after three starts in a row in which the firmware did not come up completely;
  • when the encoder button is held while the module is switched on.

In update mode the module appears on USB as a DFU device (16D0:15B7) and MuraLink lists it under Units in update mode. The LEDs show the state: LED indication. On Linux and macOS the package can be installed with dfu-util; this path is untested so far.

docs.title: USB identity
docs.text: From 26.10.1 the application identifies as 16D0:15B8 (USB Audio and the virtual COM port in one composite device) and update mode as 16D0:15B7. Firmware 26.8.0 identified as 0483:5741. Windows installs no driver for either; after the change the PC sees a new device and the COM port number can change.

In update mode the status LED and the six-LED level meter show what the bootloader does. The colours are chosen so that they cannot be mistaken for an audio level: the meter shows blue only during an update.

State Status LED Level meter Waiting for an update it was sent to; returns to the firmware by itself after 5 minutes Amber, slow blink (1 s) Dark Waiting without a timeout: no valid firmware, three failed starts, or the encoder button held at power-up Amber, fast blink (0.25 s) Dark Transfer in progress Amber, as before Fills blue, one LED per 18 % Installed, restarting Green, steady All six blue Failed Red, blinking Frozen where it stopped Transfer aborted, cable pulled, idle timeout Back to the waiting pattern Dark

The module does not show the cause of a failure; MuraLink reads it from the module and names it. Blinking pauses for a moment while the bootloader erases or writes flash; the colour stays.

The other indicator patterns of the module are on Indicators and LEDs.

docs.text:

PCB 1.3 on firmware 26.8.0

A PCB 1.3 module that still runs 26.8.0 cannot take an update bundle by itself. Contact support with the module's serial number; the first update of such a module is arranged individually. Never use the old FirmwareUpdater or DIP switch 3 on a module that runs 26.10.1 or later.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Windows 10 or 11 PC with MuraLink 26.10.1 or newer (Install).
  • The update bundle of the release, for example JPx_Update_26.10.1.zip from Downloads.
  • A USB-C data cable to the module's USB DATA connector. Charge-only cables do not work.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Connect the module in MuraLink and open Device > Firmware update.
  2. Click Open bundle and choose the .zip. MuraLink checks the file and shows the release it contains, with its variant (release, special build or development).
  3. Read the checks against the connected module: board supported, installed version and variant, key type, rollback floor. A blocking check names what is wrong and disables the update; a warning asks for your confirmation.
  4. On PCB 1.4, MuraLink asks whether to write the default DSP program as well. It replaces the DSP program that runs now, your own design included; decline to keep yours. See Boot memory with MuraLink.
  5. Confirm. The audio stops, the module restarts into update mode, and MuraLink finds it again by itself.
  6. Watch the phases: Waiting for the unit, Checking, Installing, Verifying, Restarting, Reconnecting, and Writing the DSP program if you chose it. Do not unplug the cable or switch the module off.
  7. MuraLink reconnects and shows the new version. The settings are kept; the first start after an update from 26.8.0 rebuilds the stored settings once, see Release notes 26.10.1.
Device > Firmware update before a bundle is opened.

The whole update takes about a minute, longer with the DSP program.

docs.title: If something is refused
docs.text:
MuraLink names the cause in plain terms. The usual ones:

Message Meaning What to do Board not supported by this release The bundle's manifest does not list your board Use the bundle of a release that lists it Package needs a development bootloader A development package on a production module Use the release bundle Older than the module's security floor The package's security counter is below the floor Use a newer release Secure bootloader missing The module runs 26.8.0 or older Contact support

docs.title: If the update is interrupted
docs.text: Nothing is damaged. The module waits in update mode; MuraLink lists it under Units in update mode. Open the bundle again and repeat the update. See Recovery.

docs.title: The module waits in update mode
docs.text: The status LED blinks amber quickly and the module appears in MuraLink under Units in update mode instead of as a connected device. This happens after an interrupted update, when the installed firmware failed its check, or when the firmware did not come up three times in a row. Open the update bundle and install it; the module restarts with the new firmware.

docs.title: The module does not react at all
docs.text:
1. Switch the module off.
  2. Hold the encoder button and switch the module on. Release the button once the status LED blinks amber: the bootloader is in update mode.
  3. Install the update bundle from MuraLink.

If the module does not enter update mode this way, the fault is not in the firmware. Contact support with the module's serial number.

docs.title: A PCB 1.3 module
docs.text: The same applies from firmware 26.10.1 on. Do not use the old FirmwareUpdater and do not move DIP switch 3: see Configuration.

The module carries a LinkPlay A31 Wi-Fi streaming module. It is set up and controlled with the 4STREAM app (iOS and Android), and the module plays what it receives when the Wi-Fi input is selected. This section shows what the Wi-Fi module can do, how to set it up and how to test it.

docs.title: What the Wi-Fi module can do
docs.text:
Feature What it means AirPlay Play from an iPhone, an iPad or a Mac to the module. This is AirPlay of the first generation. Spotify Connect Pick the module as the device in the Spotify app (Spotify Connect). Needs a Spotify Premium account. DLNA and UPnP Play music files from a phone, a PC or a NAS on the local network with a DLNA or UPnP player. Streaming services in the 4STREAM app Spotify, TIDAL, Qobuz, Amazon Music, SoundCloud, TuneIn, iHeartRadio, Napster and internet radio, chosen and controlled in the app. Multiroom Several modules on one network are grouped in the 4STREAM app and play in sync, or each plays its own source (Several modules together).

Not supported by this Wi-Fi module: AirPlay 2, TIDAL Connect (TIDAL plays through the 4STREAM app), Chromecast and voice assistants.

The firmware does not take part in the streaming. It selects the Wi-Fi input, follows the volume during playback (Volume and encoder) and reports what the Wi-Fi module plays: MuraLink shows the input mode, the playback state and the track on Wi-Fi > Playback, and WIFI:INPUT? answers the active mode (AIRPLAY, DLNA, SPOTIFY_CONNECT and others, see the WIFI reference).

The on-board Wi-Fi streaming module is set up with the 4STREAM mobile app. The procedure resets the module to its factory defaults, connects your phone to its temporary access point, and joins the module to your home network.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The 4STREAM app on your phone.
  • A Wi-Fi antenna connected to the module (mandatory for Wi-Fi operation).
  • The module powered and the Wi-Fi input selected (status LED white).

docs.title: Factory reset and access point mode
docs.text:
1. Start a factory reset of the Wi-Fi module: hold the encoder button with the Wi-Fi input selected until the white status LED starts blinking; or click Factory reset on MuraLink's Wi-Fi > Status and confirm; or send WIFI:RELOAD over the control interface.
  2. Wait about 20 seconds to one minute for the module to restart and open its temporary Wi-Fi network.
  3. On the phone, connect to the Wi-Fi network whose name contains "A31Audio" or "SoundSystem".
  4. Open the 4STREAM app; the device appears once the phone is on the module's access point.

docs.title: Joining your home Wi-Fi network
docs.text:
1. In the app, select the discovered device.
  2. Choose the option to add or configure a new Wi-Fi network for the device.
  3. Select your home network and enter its password.
  4. Confirm. The device leaves its own access point and joins your network; it no longer appears as a separate Wi-Fi network afterwards.

MuraLink's Wi-Fi > Status shows the Connection state and the Signal strength once the module is on your network; over the control interface WIFI:NETSTATE? and WIFI:SIGNALSTR? answer the same (WIFI reference).

Wi-Fi > Status.

If the device does not appear in 4STREAM, repeat the factory reset, check the antenna, and make sure the status LED shows the Wi-Fi input. Continue with Spotify Connect to test playback.

A quick playback test once the module is on your network (Setup with 4STREAM).

  1. Open Spotify and start playback of any track.
  2. Open the "Select a device" menu (usually in the lower right corner of the player).
  3. Select the newly set-up Wi-Fi device from the list.
  4. With the Wi-Fi input selected on the module, audio plays through the module.

If the device is missing from the list, repeat the Wi-Fi setup, check the antenna, and make sure the module's status LED shows the Wi-Fi input (white). Playing to the module also wakes it from the power-down levels that keep the Wi-Fi module powered (Power levels).
